en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Master Yuejiang, the Yuwang (King of Nurturing):
When I first traveled to study under various masters, Chan Master Yuejiang had already emerged into the world to preach the Dharma.

Although we were honored to have been friends for over thirty years, it was my regret that I did not join his assembly of disciples and remain long by his hearth and forge. During the Zhizhi era, I... [received] the... [Recorded Sayings].
When I ascended the seat at Zhijin Mountain, I had the fortune to hear his formal teachings; I was struck by how they were as boundless as the Milky Way.
Recently, his disciple Ruyue showed me the Master’s recorded sayings (*yulu*). Upon beginning to read them, I felt a sense of liberation, like a sick person meeting Qi Yu:
without recourse to decoctions, pills, acupuncture, moxibustion, or compresses, in the mere blink of an eye or a single breath, [the ailment was cured].
Having quickly departed, he returned to his natural state; his hundred limbs were harmoniously adjusted, and he forgot even that he possessed a body.

Thereupon, maintaining his spirit and stabilizing his breath, he again followed the shores to enter deeply into the ocean of nature. It is so vast as to have no exterior, and so subtle as to have no interior.

Within, there is no self-mind; without, there are no myriad objects. From the fulfillment of awakening on the ten stages above, down to the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms below, all are but the reflections and shadows of the holy and the mundane, the manifestations of transformative teachings and arrangements.

Within the ocean of the fundamental nature, they are neither existent nor non-existent, neither persisting nor perishing, neither grasped nor discarded, neither coming nor going. They are like empty space, which contains all forms, and like the great earth.

It contains and carries all things, without distinction between self and other, and without difference between past and present. Within this, one plays freely in both horizontal and vertical directions, rolling up and unfolding with sovereign ease.

Whether wielding the staff or shouting "Ho!", raising an eyebrow or blinking an eye, whether moving or still, speaking or silent, laughing, smiling, raging, or reviling—all are nothing but wondrous function.
At times giving and at times taking; at times letting loose and at times capturing; at times bestowing without any boundaries or constraints, suddenly...
Yet the cliff is severed; striking the void produces sound. To speak where there is no speech is like stirring the embers to seek bubbles; to act where there is no action is likewise so.

When he speaks in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), thunder and rain fill the eight directions; when he acts in accordance with the nature of reality, he molds the myriad transformations.
Alas! How is it that this old man performs such a great Dharma-giving? Do his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and samādhis truly manifest in such a way? From my own shallow and humble perspective...

Even so, the benefits obtained are immeasurable. Furthermore, how could there not be those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna who, upon hearing or seeing it even once, personally realize and truly awaken to it, thereby continuing the life of wisdom and transmitting the True Dharma Eye—just as the ancient stupa master did when reading the records of Yunmen?
This is sufficient evidence.
Written on the third month of the sixth year of the Zhìyuán era, the Gēngchén year, by the monk Dàxīn, resident of Lóngxiáng Monastery.
Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Master Yuèjiāng.
Composed by the junior disciple Bhikṣu Zhengcheng of Mount Jizu.
To begin with, ultimate truth has no fixed locus, and the supreme sound transcends the ordinary. Yet, there is no place where truth does not pervade, and no aspect that the sound does not encompass.
To expand upon and fulfill this, one must await the emergence of a bodhisattva of vast eras. The Master’s essential teachings are the very essence of ultimate truth and the supreme sound.
This refers to the sovereign freedom of the vast and magnificent capacity of the mind. It is like the ocean tide scattering snow;
the swift and profound eloquence is as natural as the thunderous resonance of the celestial drum. Its fundamental principles are so vast that their beginning and end cannot be fathomed.

It is like an empty valley responding to an echo or a great bell answering a strike; it is surely a matter of responding to whatever is struck within its void and penetration—how could any trace or mark ever be made manifest? Now, at this time...
This compilation was not the original intention of the Master. These Chan practitioners have gathered [the fragments] to form this volume;
it is but a single drop from the vast ocean, a mere hair-tip from Mount Tai or Mount Hua. I have briefly presented this preface to mark the time. The third year of Zhizhi, the year of Guihai.
The Day of the First Month.

The Recorded Sayings of Master Yuejiang, Volume One:
The Record of Master Yuejiang’s First Residence at Biyun Chan Temple in Changzhou Prefecture,
Compiled by his Disciple Ju Jian, Abbot of Taiping Chan Temple in Pingjiang Prefecture.
On the twentieth day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Yuanzhen era (the year of Yimwei), the Master accepted an invitation to enter the temple.
Pointing to the mountain gate, he said: "The three gates are all open; through every gate one may enter. Those of superior capacity who understand the Way shall join hands and return together."
Taking up the memorial submitted by the President, he wields the ancient ruler and measure and grasps the great scales and balance. Pearls turn and jade rolls; like thunder rolling and wind blowing.

Ascending the seat, he takes up the incense and says: "This one portion of incense is offered collectively to wish for the Ten Thousand Years, the Ten Thousand Times Ten Thousand Years of the present Emperor. Next, taking up the incense, he says: 'I burn this toward the furnace as an offering to my..."
He visited Huayan Daoheshang, Chan Master Fohui Dingzhi of Xingsheng Wanshou Chan Temple on Mount Jing, to repay the kindness of his dharma-mother.
He then took his seat. A monk asked: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind does he succeed? The Master said:
"Having eyes but no ears, sitting by the fire in the sixth month. The monk pressed further: "The official will not permit it..."

Zhennan said, "I privately communicate with carriages and horses. The Master said, "For now, I hope you, the Acharya, will transmit this well. Zhennan asked, "Regarding the Way of the Three Sages: 'When I meet people, I come forth;
when I come forth, I do not act for the sake of others'—what is the meaning of this? The Master said, "The arms are long, but the sleeves of the robe are short.
Zhennan asked, "Xinghua said, 'When I meet people, I do not come forth; when I come forth, I immediately act for others. What about that? The Master... [replied].
[The Master] said, "Your feet are thin; your straw sandals are wide. The monk stepped forward and asked, "When a Master appears in the world, does he act for the sake of people, or not?

The Master replied, "In my heart I bear no grudge against anyone; on my face I have no color of shame. The monk bowed. The Master then said, "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they see the hare and release the hawk.
When the Patriarchs came from the West, they struck the gavel at the seat of the Dharma-image. If we rely upon the gate of the patch-robed monks, it is precisely right to [act thus]."
It has been buried in a pit. Therefore, when Upper Seat Master Yin saw the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, he was like one meeting a born enemy;
when he heard the Way and heard Chan, it was like the wind passing through trees.

Today, finding no foothold, he was pushed by others into the herd of water-buffaloes, where he could not avoid tossing and spitting, scattering earth and raising dust, tearing open the crown-gates of the thousand sages, and shattering [the barriers].
At this moment, in his lair, he brandishes his staff and says: "Master Bajiao is coming! If you have a staff, I give you a staff;
if you have no staff, I take your staff away. He plants the staff on the ground and says:
"The splendor of Mount Hua spreads across the heavens; the Yellow River flows forth in its singular clarity."

Again, it is recorded that the King of Min invited Luoshan to ascend the hall. As soon as Luoshan took his seat, he gathered up his saṃghāṭī robe with his hand, looked over the assembly, and immediately descended from the seat.
The King of Min stepped forward, took Luoshan’s hand, and said, "The single assembly on Vulture Peak—"
"How is this different from today? Luoshan said, "I thought you were just an ordinary layman. The Master said, "Excellent, O virtuous Chan practitioners!
When the ruler and his minister find harmony, illumination and function are simultaneous; gain and loss are both forgotten, and right and wrong are extinguished.

But as for Luoshan saying, 'I thought you were just an ordinary layman'—what does that mean? When a chess player meets an opponent of equal skill, it is difficult to hide one's moves. [The text ends with] "The zither..."
When you meet one who understands, it is precisely the time to play.

Entering the hall [the Master said]: "The Old Man with the Yellow Face, two thousand years ago, took a single threadless cord and tied down the entire ocean-world of the ten directions—sentient and insentient alike—at the soles of their feet. This he called 'Summer Retreat' (Anju)."
Regarding this Dharma-gate of the *kaṭhina* (the summer retreat), to this day there has not yet been one who has fully mastered it.

Is there here any monk of natural integrity, one of exceptional caliber and versatile adaptability? I wish to ask you: for what reason do you put on your seven-strip robe upon hearing the sound of the bell?
Ascending the hall, he held up a stone and showed it to the assembly, saying, "I, this mountain monk, have opened a divination shop to judge people's poverty or wealth, life or death.
A monk then asked, "Setting aside poverty, wealth, life, and death, and not falling into the five elements, I pray that the Master will point directly to it.
The Stone said, "Gold, wood, water, fire, and earth. [The Master] commented: "From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old down to all the elder monks in the world, they are all simply this."
The fortune-teller Fu Shi pointed this way, yet it is rare indeed to encounter one who truly understands.

This monk intended to pass through the heavy barrier, but unwittingly he struck his head and bumped his forehead. As for what Fu Shi said—“Gold, wood, water, fire, and earth”—how do you understand it?
“Recognize the meaning at the tip of the hook; do not fixate on the zero point of the scale.”
Ascending the hall, he spoke with words that cut like a sharp chisel and removed the film from one’s eyes. Baizhang went deaf; Huangbo stuck out his tongue.

Ascending the hall, he cited Master Dongshan Kong, who addressed the assembly, saying: “I dwell at Xuefeng with fifteen hundred followers. There is no soft, faceless pancake to wrap around the pillar;
bite it horizontally or vertically, and when you are full, stop. Do not rely on others’ gates or lean upon others’ doors. Mountain.
The monastic community is not like this: they wear their cassocks inside out while singing songs of snow; they carry their straw hats upside down as they hasten to village feasts.
They know only to follow custom and eat their fill of rice, or to earn three coins to buy straw sandals.
Ascending the hall, he raised his whisk and said, "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable subtle meanings are all contained within the tip of this whisk.
Do you see them? He struck the whisk and said, "In the kingdom of Great China, the drums are beaten and the bells ring;
in the land of Silla, they offer greetings and inquire after your well-being. Now tell me, for what reason did Master Zhaozhou travel on pilgrimage for eighty years?
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Within these ninety days, I, Biyun, have been guarding the city of the mind with you all.
Nothing is allowed to go out from within; nothing is allowed to enter from without. India and this land are both contained right here.
The wax man, the ice, the iron ball, and the 'true person of no station'—what are they but dried dung? *Hē!*"

On the anniversary of the Sage’s birthday, the assembly rose from their seats following the conclusion of the service. Heaven and earth were in harmonious accord; the sun and moon shone with radiant splendor;

a pervasive aura of harmony wafted through the air, and auspicious clouds gathered in profusion. Thus, the Sage, mounted upon the wheel of his great vow, manifested birth and descended into this Jambudvīpa world.
He governs while draped in ceremonial robes, occupying the position of the Nine and Five—the most supreme and noble—unifying the ten directions as an auspicious omen and a sign of good fortune.

He transmits his fragrance across a thousand ages and surpasses a hundred kings in his glorious achievements. His benevolence encompasses the nine realms, and his compassion covers the eight quarters.
He fans the pure winds of Pangu and the Great Antiquity, and spreads the impartial, ultimate transformation of Fuxi and Xuanyuan; thus, his Way is unsurpassed and his virtue peerless.
The Virtuous Sound: His virtue was capable of illumination. Being capable of illumination, he was capable of classification; being capable of leadership, he was capable of kingship.

He ruled this great state with such success that all were submissive and united. Spontaneously, dragons roared and mist arose; tigers howled and the wind followed. Sweet springs gushed forth, and auspicious grain grew.
The phoenix arrives and the qilin appears; blessings flow through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and longevity equals that of a hundred billion Mount Merus.
At such a time as this, how can one ultimately proclaim it? He raises his whisk and says: "Holding up the unperforated flute of Shaolin, he blows forth the 'Ten-Thousand-Year Joy' against the wind."

Ascending the hall, he said: "When knowledge and views establish further knowledge, this is the root of ignorance. When knowledge and views are themselves without seeing, this is Nirvana—taintless, truly pure.
How could there be room for any other thing within it? [The Master] picked up the staff and said: "Śākyamuni’s twelve joints of bone have been smashed to pieces.
The whole family pays no heed to matters of rise and fall; they have won the right to occupy the Dongting Lake amidst the clouds."
Ascending the hall, he raised the case: Yunmen said, "The eyelashes span across the ten directions; the eyebrows above pierce through heaven and earth, while below they penetrate the Yellow Springs.
Mount Sumeru blocks your throat. Is there anyone who understands this? If there is someone who understands it—"
He drags in Campā and engages in a forehead-to-forehead clash with Silla. He comments: "Master Yunmen first terrified people to death;
later, he made people laugh to death. If anyone can understand this, they shall laugh for thirty years."
The Recorded Sayings of National Teacher Yuejiang while Residing at Dianshan Chan Temple in Songjiang;
Compiled by his disciple Miaoxin as the Abbot of Xuanhua Chan Temple in Huzhou Prefecture.
On the twelfth day of the seventh month in the seventh year of the Dade era (the Gui-mao year), the Master received [the appointment].
At the request of the Xingxuan Yuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs), he entered the temple.
Arriving at the Buddha Hall, he said: "The Buddhas of the past were disciples of the Buddhas of the present. Of whom are the Buddhas of the present the disciples?
Raising his sitting mat, he said: "In one lift, forty-nine."

[The Master] held up the temple’s formal address (*shu*). "To proclaim and circulate virtuous governance is truly in accord with ultimate impartiality. To fully uphold a single phrase is to universally respond to all capacities.

Having finished offering incense to pray for the Emperor, he took his seat. A monk asked: "The *dharma-flower* manifests once more; the spring returns to the garden of awakening. At this very moment—"
[The monk] requested the Master to offer a prayer for the Sage. The Master said, "The benevolence of Yao is like Heaven.
The monk stepped forward and asked, "What is the primary meaning? The Master said, "This is the secondary meaning. The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall scatter the assembly with a shout!
The Master said, "A lion bites a man; a hunting dog chases a clod of earth. The monk bowed. The Master then said, "Sitting upright in the light of day, the true command is fully manifest."
The sun shines upon the heavens; the rivers are clear and the seas are tranquil. In every atom and every realm, the wondrous gate of all Buddhas is fully revealed.
In every object and every situation, it is entirely the realm of Universal Light. This extensively displays the true eye for humans and devas; this turns the fundamental wheel of Dharma.
By this, the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom is continued; by this, the lamp of the patriarchs is transmitted and maintained; by this, the national ethos is assisted and supported.
This serves to assist in propagating the supreme transformation. Holding up his staff, he said: "Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, a jade flute is blown;
beneath the Ten-Thousand-Year Pine, a golden bell is struck. He brought the staff down once with a sharp tap.
Again, he raised this case: A monk asked Touzi, "What is the one great matter of causal conditions?
Touzi replied, "The Minister Yin invited the old monk to open the hall. The Master commented, "Śākyamuni Buddha entrusted the Buddha-dharma to kings and great ministers."

A powerful donor has enabled the Dharma to endure for a long time. Master Touzi, whose voice resonated like a great flood from the primordial antiquity, poured down the rain of Dharma upon this sacred land.
Thus, the Milky Way shone brilliantly and the golden ramparts were made secure. Today, someone suddenly asks Dianshan, "What is this one great matter of causal conditions?
To which he simply replies: "The Imperial Commissioner Cao requests that I, this mountain monk, [speak]."
The hall was opened. Now tell me: is this the same as the ancients, or is it different? He raised his staff and struck once.
"One sees only the imperial wind forming a single expanse; one knows not where the boundaries lie."
The posthumous letter from my late teacher, the Buddha-Wisdom of Mount Jing, has arrived. I offer incense.

On the second day of the seventh month, at the beginning of autumn, the Vairambha wind rolls through the void and the waters of the sea stand up; it blows down the First Peak of Lingxiao until even the gods wail and the ghosts weep.

If one says my late teacher has entered extinction, it is a grievous injustice to the Blue Heaven. If one says my late teacher has not entered extinction, the Blue Heaven suffers a grievous injustice.
A slap across the jaw; three punches under the ribs. Thinking back on this now with a cold heart, I regret not having settled this grievance at the outset.

When the Dharma instructions reached the time for the ascent to the hall, a monk asked: "Son of the Buddha from the Western Heaven, Imperial Preceptor of the Great Yuan—your fame resounds through the five [directions]..."

"O Celestial One! Your transformations spread throughout the eight directions. At such a time as this, who is it that knows your grace? The Master said, "The Dharma-thunder rolls far and wide, and the many dragons rejoice;
the Sun of Wisdom has just begun to rise, and the great earth is illumined. The student continued, "Where the lion roars, the cubs grow vigorous;

when the Dharma-rain falls in torrents, the trees flourish. The Master said, "The sun and moon are impartial. The student continued, "Zhongguo Shī [National Teacher Zhong] was once asked by Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty..."
Zong asked, "What is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies? The National Teacher said, "Donor, you are treading upon the crown of Vairocana;
what is your intention? The Master said, "I have the fortune to gaze up at him. He pressed further, "The Emperor said, 'What is the meaning of this? What did the National Teacher mean by that?
The National Teacher said, "Do not mistake it for your own pure Dharma-body. "How can one thoroughly understand this? the Master asked. The National Teacher said, "I report it with my bare heart."
The Master said, "Just this morning, the Dharma edict was proclaimed far and wide; humans and devas alike look up to it with reverence. How will you, Preceptor, repay this?
The Master said, "Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. The Master said, "Only by knowing gratitude can one understand how to repay it. He then bowed.
The Master then said: "The Great Function manifests before us; the Great Capacity responds perfectly. It is like the sky universally covering all, like the earth universally supporting all.
It is like the moon illuminating a thousand rivers, like spring circulating through ten thousand lands. I myself am originally without mind and have nothing to seek;
yet now this great treasure of the Dharma King arrives spontaneously. It truly brings about the movement of clouds and the falling of rain, with thunderous vigor and the soaring of winds."
The Dharma transforms and all quarters are at peace; the profound resonance vibrates and the four seas are tranquil.
Demons and heretics thus hide their traces, while humans and devas rejoice together from this moment on. At such a time as this, to whom ultimately does the merit belong?
May we, like the Venerable Baozhang, live for a thousand years, remaining eternally so through ten thousand ages.

The Teacher of Emperors ascends the hall on the first day of the year. This is the beginning of the year, the beginning of the day; from this beginning, the myriad transformations commence, and upon this beginning, the great earth abides.
From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity down to the elder monks of the world, they have poured forth like rivers and surged like oceans to speak of this beginning.
The character does not emerge from the trichiliocosm, nor even from the Flower Treasury Sea of Worlds; though one exhausts this primordial character, it remains inexhaustible.
This mountain monk offers but a single phrase to you all, and then descends from the seat.

Ascending the hall on the first full moon of the year: before the lamp is lit and after the lamp is lit, there is no distinction between inner and outer throughout all time; space has no front or back.
At the Aranya Monastery in the Western Heaven, when a flower from the lamp fell to the ground and burned the eyebrows of Śakra, it was you people who were there.
"Do you still feel your face burning with heat?
He ascended the hall and said: "Those who 'pelt a dead sparrow on the ground' are as numerous as hemp or millet.
Those who, upon being shouted at, strike out into the void—such masters are rarely encountered. This mountain monk’s single staff has never been lightly brought forth; were it not for those above..."
"A superior person has arrived. How shall one move him? You must know that the Buddha-dharma is no small matter.
He ascended the hall and cited Master Pang: "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action.
This is the field for selecting Buddhas; with an empty mind, they return as the valedictorians. He added: "A shrimp leaps up to the Brahma Heaven; an earthworm brushes past the East."
The Sea.
Upon the conclusion of the Qingmiao Assembly, he ascended the hall and said: "A nation takes its people as its foundation; the people take food as their heaven.
For us patch-robed monks, wisdom is our life and the joy of Zen is our sustenance. Today, I and all of you have spent these days together wandering through the Vairocana [universe]."
That ocean of nature has traversed all one hundred and ten cities; regarding the spiritual friends he consulted and the Dharma gates he attained, there is nothing he does not fully know.
But tell me: what Dharma was discussed between the presiding deity of the exquisite flavor of softness and the countless presiding deities of the harvest?
[The Master] raises his staff, strikes once, and says: "Return to the hall for tea."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Xuansha did not cross the ridge; Baoshou did not ford the river; the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven; Bodhidharma did not come to this eastern land.
Thus they dwelt in retreat, thus they observed the *jinzu* (foot-binding) period. Under the gate of this mountain monastery, three thousand blows are struck at dawn."
Evening: Eight hundred blows.
Entering the hall: Generally speaking, for every question and answer, every press and push, one must be a practitioner of the true lineage before being fit to engage in such discourse.
Bring me even half a piece of Yunmen’s “moldy cake,” and I will give you half a Mount Sumeru.
"You have brought Zhaozhou’s cup of tea; I shall give you a drop of the great ocean's water.
If Mount Sumeru cannot enter your eyes, and the great ocean's water cannot enter your ears, then do not mistakenly blame others."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Coming from the south, coming from the north; carrying up, carrying down. What is the price of rice in Luling? To whom shall the money for the straw sandals be paid?
If you do not probe the dragon’s jaw, how can you obtain the dragon pearl? If you do not enter the tiger’s den, how can you seize the tiger cub?
He struck the meditation seat and rose.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "When one recites hymns on the bell tower and plants vegetables beneath the bed frame, what is the meaning?
The Master said, "There is no meaning. The monk pressed further: "The wind does not whistle through the branches; the rain does not break the clods of earth. What a fine time of peace this is!

The Master said, "Those who recognize this grace are few. The Master then continued: "The wind does not whistle through the branches; the rain does not break the clods of earth. On the bell tower, one recites..."
Praise! Underneath the bed, vegetables were growing. Last night, Śakra, Lord of Devas, was in the courtyard arguing with Deshan and Linji over the Buddha-dharma.
Provoked by their profound and wondrous divine power, he seized Mount Sumeru and smashed it to pieces with a single blow of his mallet.
I, this mountain monk, was startled awake from my dream; without realizing it, I rose and clapped my hands, laughing out loud "ha ha. But tell me, what was there to laugh about?
Two thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, bhikṣus have little sense of shame.
When the First Patriarch offered incense, he said: "The Southern Heaven is not my place of birth; the Eastern Land is likewise not my field of transformation.

The steep ridges of Mount Xi are so remote that all traces of departure are lost; the Shaolin groves are so silent that not even a shadow of winter is seen. But tell me: does the Patriarch return today?
[He said: "None. Holding up a censer, he said: "The five-petaled flower blooms in a spring beyond the kalpas; who will listen to this single note of rare sound? Ascending the hall, [he said]:
"Dongshan’s 'three pounds of flax,' Zhaozhou’s 'pine tree'—a mosquito on an iron ox: there is no place for you to open your beak.
You monks, today the third and tomorrow the fourth, simply know how to follow the custom and eat your fill. This, too, is acceptable.
"Three coins bought me straw sandals.
He ascended the hall, held up his staff, and said: "O staff! Two thousand years ago at the assembly on Vulture Peak, you personally heard the Tathāgata’s golden mouth issue this earnest instruction:
that after two thousand years have passed, you shall cause all bhikṣus to rely upon the Bodhisattva Vehicle and cultivate tranquility."
The Practice of Cessation: Just now, he departed for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and traveled throughout the boundless seas of fragrant water.
He then circled Mount Sumeru three times before returning to his original location. For the sake of all people, he spoke these verses on the Summer Retreat (*an-guo*):
"All people fear the scorching heat, Yet I delight in the lengthening summer days. A fragrant breeze blows from the south, Bringing a subtle coolness to the palace halls. — By Zhuo Zhujia.
[The Master] strikes the gavel once. He ascends the hall.
A monk asks, "What is the Buddha-dharma at the beginning of the New Year? The Master says, "Great snow fills Chang'an.
The monk steps forward and asks, "What if the sun suddenly rises? The Master says, "You have deceived yourself, O Kalyāṇamitra. The Master then says, "The New Year is spread abroad."

An edict is issued. As the four seasons begin anew, a thousand mountains are white with snow and ten thousand ravines are cold with mist. The great earth, its rivers and mountains, all bow their heads together as the court ranks form in the morning at the Purple Palace Hall.
Ascending the hall, he said: "In all quarters, the staff and the shout are taken as the Buddha-work; at Puguang, the staff and the shout are placed high on a shelf.

In all quarters, the banners and drums of the great general are raised; at Puguang, the banners and drums are set aside against the wall. To anyone who comes, it is merely a matter of ordinary meeting;
naturally, the roles of guest and host are clearly defined. Do you understand? This is the imperial decree of the Golden Wheel Emperor—the house style of the thatched-roof shop."
Separate Record of the Sayings of Venerable Yuejiang while Residing at Xingguo Chan Temple in Songjiang.
Compiled by his disciple Daji, Abbot of Xianci Chan Temple in Huzhou Prefecture.
The Buddha hall. The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. Three catties of hemp. A dried piece of excrement. The very bottom of the hall.
Eighty-one (nine times nine). Then, pay homage.
Small Assembly. A monk asked, "The Dharma follows the practice of the Dharma; the banner of the Dharma is established wherever it may be.
To whom does this matter belong? The Master said, "Pǔ. The monk stepped forward and said, "Today I have heard what I had not heard before. The Master said, "Zhá! The Master then said:
In the palace of Magadha, there was no passage for water to flow through; within the city of Vaiśālī, the paths were laid open.
At times, atop solitary peaks, he roared at the moon and slept amidst the clouds; at other times, in the middle of the crossroads, he mixed mud with water.

Therefore, when this mountain monk dwells on Mount Duan, he sees only the realm of Mount Duan: the shimmering ripples of the lake’s light and the swaying shadows of the trees, with the grasses of the ravines and the cliffs.

Flowers; the songs of woodcutters and the chants of fishermen come from Xingguo. One sees only the local customs of Xingguo: tides flow through a hundred estuaries, and the moon illuminates ten thousand homes.
Cranes cry out amidst the clouds; orioles sing among the ancient trees. Across a hundred cities of misty waters, there is no second Mañjuśrī.
When the gates of the pavilions open, who is named Maitreya? [The Master] strikes his whisk: "The Persian’s nostrils are long."
Ascending the hall: These ninety days of a summer retreat have passed in a mere trice. Some take the wax man as their proof; others take the iron ball as their proof.
This is like a group of blind men feeling an elephant, or a skilled butcher disassembling an ox—none of them have yet seen the principle of the whole elephant or the whole ox.
Xuedou said: "The whole elephant and the whole ox are no different from the cataracts [obscuring the eye]; from of old, the masters have shared this name."

Master Xuefeng said, "The entire great earth is this gate of liberation; I hold out my hand to pull you in, yet you will not enter. Now tell me: how is it so?
Where does the intention of the ancients lie? Nowadays, most practitioners of the Way spontaneously give rise to self-defeat and create their own difficulties or ease.

They claim to have realized what they have not realized; they claim to have attained what they have not attained. Hearing sounds, they are obstructed by sounds; seeing forms, they are obstructed by forms; seeing emptiness, they are obstructed by emptiness;
seeing mountains, they are obstructed by mountains; seeing water, they are obstructed by water; seeing the Buddha, they are obstructed by the Buddha. Seeing...
When Māra is obstructed by Māra, yet desires to stride alone across the Great Square, he must transcend the Three Realms.
What are the Three Realms? Greed is the Realm of Desire; hatred is the Realm of Form; delusion is the Formless Realm. In a single thought-moment of greed, you are submerged by water;
in a single thought-moment of hatred, you are consumed by fire; in a single thought-moment of delusion, you are swept away by wind. If you can detach from these—
These three types of people are those who have transcended the three realms. Hearing sounds, they are not obstructed by sound; seeing forms, they are not obstructed by form;
seeing emptiness, they are not obstructed by emptiness; seeing mountains, they are not obstructed by mountains; seeing water, they are not obstructed by water.
Seeing the Buddha, he was not hindered by the Buddha; seeing Māra, he was not hindered by Māra. He spoke of long and short periods [of retreat], yet he was not hindered by long and short periods.
He spoke of the summer retreat and the practice of *kaṭhina*, yet he was not hindered by the summer retreat or the *kaṭhina*.
He was free in all places and unimpeded in all places. Striking the meditation seat, he said: "It is like people climbing a mountain; each must exert their own effort."
The Summer Retreat is concluded. The Golden Immortal with his iron mask—open your eyes and look at him; a chilling wind arises. Far-off mountains form his eyebrows, red apricots his cheeks.
Once the mouth is opened, one has already fallen into error. In Pūrvavideha the drum is beaten; in Jambudvīpa the small assembly is held.
In Aparagoyānī the summer retreat is kept; in Uttarakuru the invitation for self-examination is made. The sun and moon dwell in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
"Superior to benefit. In the four dhyānas, there are no calamities of wind or fire. You people sit within this realm of coolness;
how could you know that in Jiangnan and the Two Zhe regions, it is cold in spring and hot in autumn? (He lets out a shout.)
Entering the Summer Retreat. Right here is the solitary peak of Mount Miaofeng, where dragons and snakes are intermingled and ordinary beings and sages dwell together.

Those coming from the south are assigned to the upper quarters; those coming from the north are settled in the lower quarters. Their nostrils touch one another; their bare flesh presses against each other.
Those who stand like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high are as soft as a ball of cotton; those who are mixed with mud and water are forged from solid steel. Listen!
Within his belly he contains boundless seas of fragrant water; within his eyes he contains ten billion Mount Sumerus.
For ninety days, even the Buddha-eye could not look through them. It is just like the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, who sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas.
"For what reason have you not attained the Buddha-way? I will tell you when the waters of the small stream flow upstream.

The summer retreat has begun. A clear faculty rests upon the palm; the celestial bell is struck in the thirty-three heavens. When great function manifests, the drum of Guannan is beaten in the presence of all.
For a patch-robed monk, taking a single step overturns the four great seas of fragrant water, yet it is not called such.

Can one remain in *kaṭhina* (the summer retreat) by moving even a single thought? To push over ten billion Mount Sumerus with a single movement of the mind—can this not be called dwelling in the rains retreat (*an-gu*)?
Therefore it is said: "If you establish even a single speck of dust, the village elder frowns; if you do not establish even a single speck of dust, the village elder sings for joy."
At the tips of the hundred grasses, lay down your weapons; at the gate of the bustling marketplace, recognize your own self. A single moon universally appears in all waters;
all the moons in the water are subsumed within that one moon. One accomplishes eighty-four thousand gates of worldly affliction;
in a mere snap of the fingers, three lives pass as sixty kalpas.
Winter Solstice. The Buddhas of the three periods do not know it exists; a lamb-headed child pushes a bright moon. The tabby cat and the white ox, however, do know it exists;
a bottomless boat carries the morning breeze. Thoroughly illuminating the true rule beyond the categories, leaking forth the news from before the kalpas.
With phrase or without phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree—when the tree falls, the vine withers. Where do the phrases return? The short master...
"Uncle, as for selling the cotton cloth for three thousand *li*, I do not ask about that. But why, O Great Muzhou, did you set down the mud platter? Hehe! A great laugh!
[The Master] strikes the whisk. "The first line of the hexagram Yang-sheng (the Return of Yang) appears; from the winter solstice to the Cold Food Festival is one hundred and five days."
On the eve of the New Year, it is said: Days shift and months transform; the year departs and the new one arrives. Heaven is cold and people are cold;
each should take care to preserve themselves. Where can one find anyone to emulate when the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita sold his heart and liver?
Where is the news of Sudhana, who ran until his feet were covered in sores? Before the mountain lives Old Man Wang, one hundred and twenty years of age, riding upon a water buffalo.
A bull. From the southern village to the northern village; passing through the eastern village to the western village. The report says:

Gradually the skin becomes like that of a chicken and the hair like that of a crane; look and see how the gait becomes tottering. There is only the path of cultivation; simply observe this one water-bull.
Water-buffalo, water-buffalo! Four hooves trampling the earth; its hide is good for drumskins, and its horns are good for blowing—*li ming li ming*.
But tell me, what tune is this? The twenty-ninth day of the twelfth lunar month.
The Discourse Record of Master Yuejiang while Residing at Daochang Chan Temple in Huzhou, Compiled by His Disciples Huiguan, Shouchun, Dehui, and Others.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month in the second year of the Tianli era, the Master accepted his invitation and entered the temple. Pointing to the mountain gate, he said: "This..."
This is the gateway traversed by a thousand sages. If you people find a way of entry, do not fail the mountain monk.
In the Patriarch’s Hall: rock stands from within the void; fire burns within the water. The flesh of the Patriarchs is still warm.

He ascended the seat. Having finished offering incense and making prayers for the Emperor, he took his place and said: "I am originally without mind and have nothing to seek. Yet now, this precious treasury has arrived spontaneously.
Is there anyone who can peer over the fence and enter, or take their place at the cauldron and taste its contents? A monk stepped forward and asked: "Ceasing [the teachings] at Mount Miaofeng..."

At the patriarchal seat, [Zhaozhou] was seated at the site of practice on Mount Hu. A monk asked, "What is the Venerable One of Immovability? Zhaozhou replied, "An eighty-year-old man rolls a brocade ball.
The monk said, "Today you open the hall; we wish to hear your benediction. Zhaozhou replied, "When one person has cause for celebration, ten thousand people depend upon it.
The monk asked, "What is the realm of Yunfeng? Zhaozhou replied, "Before the steps, trees of girth as large as an embrace send their fragrance into the clouds."
The clear pool beneath the eaves reflects the jade mats. A monk asked, "What is it like to be a person within this realm? He replied, "His nostrils reach toward heaven; he cannot be pierced.
The monk asked, "I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding the person and the realm; as for the profound barrier beyond, what is it like?"
The answer was given: "Jade is naturally without flaw; carved patterns ruin its virtue. The monk bowed, and the Master said:
"Atop the peak of Daochang Mountain, what is at its foot? This matter belongs to one house. When the river moon shines and the pine wind blows, the true face is present.
For five hundred years, those who have occupied this seat have all been like dragons leaping and tigers bounding, like lightning rolling and stars flying—all were truly *hu* (hawks)."
With eyes like those of a hawk and a copper head and iron forehead, by the time this mountain monk arrives, you will already have lost seven or eight of them.
(He lets out a shout. The divine light is never obscured; it is a glorious legacy for all ages. Having entered this gate, do not harbor intellectual understanding.
Therefore it is said: "If I were to truly uphold and proclaim the religious teachings, I would require the grass before the Dharma Hall to be a fathom deep.
Yet, matters are not one-sided, and principles emerge in manifold ways. For now, let us convey a message through the gate of transformative teaching.
Raising his whisk, he said: "Look! Look! Amidst a heap of rubble, gold fills the ground; upon a single blade of grass, a jade palace stands."

Majestic and towering! Every particle of dust is a field of liberation; every world-system possesses a path reaching the heavens. The long-standing virtuous ones of the various mountains shall forever serve as bridges and rafts across the sea of suffering;
the elders of the two orders shall eternally act as the pillars and bedrock of the mountain gate. Thus, may the ancestral Way be gloriously illuminated once more.

The profound breeze of the Mysterious Way vibrates mightily; the green bamboos and yellow flowers alike receive this supreme transformation. Woodcutters’ songs and fishermen’s chants together rejoice in the era of ascendant peace.
At such a time as this, where ultimately does the merit reside? (He strikes the whisk. Heaven and earth are unified under new sun and moon.
The ancient mountains and rivers of the trichiliocosm sand-grains.
Again, it is cited: A monk asked Baizhang, "What is the extraordinary matter? Baizhang said, "Sitting alone on the Great Hero Peak.
The monk bowed; Baizhang then struck him. The verse says: Sitting loftily atop the Great Hero Peak, He picks up a rabbit’s horn to paint a fine picture.
Mèi: In laughter and jest, he occupies the lion’s den; who can seize my phoenix pool? A single day’s bright moon shines upon the jade table;
a full courtyard of autumn wind stirs the cassia branches. I bow my head and wish you immeasurable longevity;
may we all enjoy this time of great peace together.
That evening, during the informal discourse (xiaochan), a monk asked: "At Mount Lingyan they spoke of the moon; at Caoxi they pointed to the moon. What is the meaning of this? The Master replied:
"In times of peace and tranquility, one must strictly avoid distorted speech. The monk asked: "Regarding Master Mazu’s story of the three men admiring the moon—how do you explain that?
The Master replied: "When a single wave stirs, ten thousand waves follow. The monk asked: "One man said, 'It is precisely now that offerings should be made. Another said..."
"In the human realm, it is precisely when one is fit for practice that a man brushes his sleeves and returns to the assembly; I do not know who is superior and who is inferior.
He replied, "Everyone blows out the lamp and walks in the dark. The monk asked, "Master Mazu said, 'The sutras return to the storehouse and Chan returns to the sea;
only Puyan alone transcends the mundane world. Is this praise or is it a reproach? He replied, "A spiked iron caltrop; turn it over."
The situation became precarious. The monk prostrated. The Master then said: "Before Baizhang, there was no institution of abbotship;

they merely dwelt in caves and lived among crags, drinking from mountain streams and eating from the trees. Thus, on solitary peaks of ten thousand fathoms, where the bird-path is empty and profound, amidst the azure void and the blue heavens, such was the livelihood of the practitioners—a truly auspicious atmosphere of peace.
Without cause, they established rules and regulations, distinguishing between master and [servant]..."

Guest: Since the Great Simplicity has been diluted and the pure wind has dispersed, it has caused men of leisure—three hundred, five hundred—to build great houses and dwell therein, making a great clamor in groups of nine times nine and ten times ten, half green and half white.
Deshan and Linji flaunt their own "quince" (cha-li); Yunmen and Zhaozhou demand a price as high as the heavens. The descendants of later generations merely receive the echoes and inherit the sounds.
"Empty! To call a bell a jar is to attempt to uphold the school’s tradition of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
it is truly worlds apart from the truth. How does this compare to beneath my Yunfeng?
There, men of great virtue and advanced years each extend a hand, intending to move the palaces of Suyama and Tuṣita to the jade dais of Xuefeng. When I first entered the gate, I heard of this."
A message! Unconsciously, I began to dance with my hands and feet. Then, laughing heartily, I said: "The broom-handle that has stood for many years is now ruined;

casually picked up, it establishes the fundamental principles of the school. When ruler and subject find harmony, wind and clouds meet—this is not like the 'Eighth Young Master' of other quarters. He struck the whisk.
Again, Panshan addressed the assembly, saying: "The moon of mind is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the myriad phenomena.
The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist. When both light and objects are forgotten, what is this? [The Master] comments:
The old man Panshan, prior to the time of Vipaśyin Buddha (Viyinwang), brought forth a most extraordinary and momentous matter that is truly impenetrable to the wind and unsullied by water.
[The Master] said: "I, this mountain monk, intend to open a single eye to meet with Panshan. He struck his whisk and said: "On this night, the single orb is full;
where is its pure light not present?"
Addressing the two orders of the assembly in the hall: Ritual is not expressed without jade and silk; music is not transmitted without bells and drums.

When the pillars and limbs of the monastic community have found their proper people, the rites and music of the Three Dynasties are fully present herein. [The Master] raises his staff and says: "For all the Tathāgatas of the past, it was like the wind blowing over the grass;
for all the Bodhisattvas of the present, it is like the resonance of jade and metal; for those who practice and study in the future—"
"It cannot be lacking even by a single fraction. [The Master] strikes the sounding block once. Opening the furnace, he ascends the hall:
"At the hearth in the South, there is a saying that has neither guest nor host. It is as light as Mount Taihua, yet as heavy as a goose feather.
The Buddhas of the three periods have not spoken it; the Patriarchs of the six generations have not lifted it up. The old masters of the world..."
"O Monk! You search for it but cannot find it. This mountain monk, not begrudging his own eyebrows, shall explain it through for you all. After a long silence, he said:
"When one ox drinks water, five horses do not neigh."

The Master ascends the hall upon the completion of the Dharma Hall and Sangha Hall. A monk asks, "An ancient said, 'If one were to truly proclaim the teaching, it must be such that the grass before the Dharma Hall grows ten feet deep.
What is the meaning of this? The Master says, "A long sword leans against the sky; how cold!"
The student said, "I would rather leave the seven bays of the monks' hall empty than fear that the Buddha-Dharma might rot away. What then?

The Master said, "Throwing a brick to draw out a jade. The student said, "Tell me, does Old Chan Master Mushi’s single-minded construction of the Dharma Hall and the monks' hall compare with that of the ancients—is it the same or different? The Master said, "Do not walk where the Tathāgata has walked. The monk bowed.

[The student] bows. The Master then says: "The ultimate great is identical to the small; one does not see its boundaries or surface. The ultimate small is identical to the great; one forgets and transcends all realms.

This mountain monk takes the lands of the ten directions as his monastery, the boundless Dharma-realm as his hall, the myriad phenomena of the universe as his disciples, and the eight classes of devas and dragons as his retinue. Take one step forward and you will kick against the..."
The nostrils of King Mīṇendra take a step back and trample upon the spine of Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
Even if the Golden Ox were to dance forth with rice, Zhaozhou would immediately emerge leaning on his staff. This is precisely like a craftsman under the school of Lu Ban wielding his axe;
yet, if one wishes to see the newly forged sun and moon and the specially established heaven and earth, it must be through me, the old Chan monk Mushi. Do you understand?
"Ma! To startle the multitude, one must be a man of heroic spirit; to overcome the victor, one must be a lion’s cub.

[The Master] requested the attendants to ascend the hall. A monk asked: "What is the dharma-realm of non-obstruction of principle? He replied: "The head-dhūta rock is enveloped in moss. The monk asked:
"What is the dharma-realm of non-obstruction of phenomena? He replied: "The moon is in the water when you cup it in your hands."
[The Master] plucks flowers with his hand; the fragrance fills his robes. The monk asks, "What is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena?
He replies, "The nest knows the wind; the cave knows the rain. The monk asks, "What is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena?
He replies, "A rock stands from within the void; fire burns within the water. The monk says, "If that is so, then the patriarchs of old and those of today..."
Shang replied, "One cannot breathe through another's nostrils. The monk said, "Thank you for your answer, Master," and shook his sleeves to return to the assembly.

The Master then said, "The dharma-realm of principle; the dharma-realm of phenomena; the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena; the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena.
Raising his whisk, he asked, "What dharma-realm is this? If you do not understand, I shall give it to you further."

It is pointed out: "The scriptures return to the treasury; Chan returns to the sea. This is the dharma-realm of the Abbot (*tsang-chu*). "When a guest arrives, one must look upon them; when a thief arrives, one must ward them off.
This is the dharma-realm of the Guest Master (*chih-k'o*). "Planting vegetable roots facing upward; for two years, they share the same spring. This is the dharma-realm of the Steward (*tien-tso*).
"Reaping three hundred heads of patriarchs"—this is the dharma-realm of the Head of the Work-Team (*chih-sui*). But what is the dharma-realm of the Elder (*chang-lao*)?
The Dharma-realm. The blue-eyed barbarian monk smiles and nods his head. At this moment, this mountain monk understands nothing at all. (He strikes the whisk. Entering the hall:
Regarding the Buddha-dharma of the New Year, how shall it be guided? In the clear pool and upon the jade mat, we meet face-to-face.
Samantabhadra fastens the trousers of the Elephant King; Mañjuśrī drapes the robe of the Lion King. Now tell me, does the "True Person of No Rank" receive [it]?
"Even for a year, there is none. Once clarity is shattered, it cannot be sustained. He ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "The sun and moon dwell above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; in the fourth dhyāna, there are no calamities of wind or fire.
I wonder whose realm this is? He replied, "Hū Zhangsan and Hē Lisi. The monk said, "As for the lamp-lighting..."
[The monk] came forward and ran inside a pillar to hide himself. "Why did the Master not know [where you were]? he asked. The Master replied, "Chen the Straw Sandals; Zhou the Diamond.
The monk said, "Why did Master Yunmen instead join his palms at the mountain gate and burn incense in the Buddha hall?
The Master replied, "Ox-head to the south, Horse-head to the north. The monk bowed. The Master then said, "What a fine original!"
The Night Festival: Without oil, no lamps are lit. Heaven and Earth receive fresh rain and dew; clouds and waters are the old masters and monks.
The stone tiger turns its body; the clay ox exerts all its strength in plowing. In Great Peace there is not a single thing; at midday, the third watch is struck.
When the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he ascended the hall. [The Master] cited Emperor Shunzong of the Tang dynasty, who asked Chan Master Foguang:
"From what direction does the Buddha come? Toward what direction does he go when he passes away? Since it is said that he is always present in the world, where is the Buddha now? He replied:

"The Buddha comes from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and goes toward the unconditioned. The Dharma-body is equal to empty space; it is eternally present in the realm of no-mind. The Emperor was greatly [impressed].
Yue said: "The Dharma-body is vast and great, equal to empty space; why need one compare its arising and ceasing for similarities or differences?
After wind and rain have passed over the peach blossoms lining the road, where can a horse's hoof avoid the remaining petals?"

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: A monk asked Master Guangde Zhou, “Ajita, it is said that one who does not sever afflictions and does not cultivate meditative concentration will, according to the Buddha’s teaching, undoubtedly attain Buddhahood. How is this principle to be understood? Zhou replied, “The salt is exhausted and the charcoal is gone.
The monk asked, “What is it like when the salt is exhausted and the charcoal is gone? Zhou said, “Do not speak of your sorrows to one who is already sorrowful.”
To speak of sorrow for one already grieving is to kill them with sorrow. The verse says: Walking, I look at the mountains; sitting, I look at the mountains.
In the spring breeze, the flowers and birds warble their own songs. Since Shancai departed, no one has arrived. The gates of the pavilion stand open all day long in idleness.
Ascending the hall upon the newly completed Dharma-seat, he addressed the great assembly: "This place is the abode of Vairocana Tathāgata;
it is the Hall of Good Dharma atop Mount Sumeru, belonging to Kauśika. This seat is the Universal Radiance Treasury, the Lion Throne.
This canopy is the one offered by the Elder Ratnakūṭa, which completely covers the three thousandfold world system."
The thousandfold world-system: its seat rises eighty-four thousand yojanas high, and its hall is one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas high.
Each window, each railing, and each treasury of adornment interlace their radiance with one another like nets of precious threads;
they are like the pores of Samantabhadra and like the pavilions of Maitreya, manifesting within every single ocean of Buddha-fields.
It is unprecedented, unimpaired, and unmixed. For it was here that all Buddhas of the past entered this hall; therefore, this hall is most solemn and pure.
It was here that all Buddhas of the past sat upon this seat; therefore, this seat is most auspicious. It was here that all Buddhas of the past accepted this precious parasol;
therefore, this parasol is most extraordinary. One must know that this hall, this seat, and this parasol do not originate from the heavens.
It descends, yet does not emerge from the earth; it issues forth entirely from the fundamental wisdom of the ancient Chan master Moshi of my mountain.
Vertically exhausting the three periods of time, the three periods are thus perfectly interfused; horizontally spanning the ten directions, the ten directions are thus universally unobstructed.
[The Master] strikes the whisk. "The void can be measured, the wind can be struck, but none can fully describe the Buddha’s merit.
Ascending the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony, a monk asks: "The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories;

why then did he descend to be born in the royal palace? The Master replies: "Do not slander Gautama. The monk says: "But what about his pointing to heaven and pointing to earth? The Master replies: "Yellow..."
[The Master] stopped the child’s crying with a leaf. The monk said, "I do not yet understand: for what reason do the Buddhas appear in the world?
He replied, "Where Li Lou walks, the waves overflow the heavens. The Master then said: "If anyone wishes to enter the realm of the Buddha, they should purify their mind like empty space;
remaining far removed from discursive thoughts and all grasping, they shall cause the mind to be unimpeded wherever it turns. All you virtuous practitioners of meditation!"
If you pick up the ladle, you are obstructed by the ladle. If you wash this one, you cannot wash that one; you are then obstructed by that one.
If you wash that one, you cannot wash this one; you are then obstructed by this one.
How can you attain a state where there is no obstruction in whatever direction you turn? Speak of it before Prince Siddhārtha had even emerged from his mother’s womb.
"Come with one phrase.
Empress Taramaśrī bestows robes and ascends the hall. "Kāśyapa’s upper robe, the crest-jewel of the Wheel-Turning King—having obtained it, it was originally without intention;
where it is worn, its length and breadth are perfectly suited. Furthermore, what is this 'repaying virtue and recompensing grace'?"
The phrase of grace: Last night the sun-disk opened its chrysanthemums; this morning the moon-cave gave birth to *zhicao* fungi.
When the Abbot prepared the vegetarian feast and ascended the hall, Yunmen ate the sesame cakes and bit into the nostrils of Śakra;
Yungfeng ate the leftovers and bit into the tongue of Kauṇḍinya. All of you, during the two sessions of the day, ascend the hall to eat porridge and rice.

How is it when there is cooperation? Suddenly, one bites through a piece of iron-crusty sour pastry and only then realizes that Indra’s nostrils are nothing but Kātyāyanīputra’s tongue, and Kātyāyanīputra’s tongue is nothing but Indra’s nostrils.
Have you not seen it said: "The wisdom of all-knowledge is pure; it is non-dual, without duality, without distinction, and without interruption"? *Hah!* (A shout)
"Ha! [The Master] ascends the hall. A monk asks, "What is the body of the thousand-foot Śākyamuni? The Master says, "Fat, it does not reveal the flesh;
thin, it does not reveal the bone. The monk presses further, "What is the body of sixteen feet of purple-gold color? The Master says, "Avoid this at all costs."
"Recognizing a slave as a lord. The student said, "Preceptor, do not force the noble to become base. The Master said, "I have always been a Liu Xiaohui.
The Master then said, "Sometimes I take a whisk made of tortoise hair and treat it as a sixteen-foot golden body;
sometimes I take a sixteen-foot golden body and treat it as a whisk made of tortoise hair. Seven tops and eight bottoms, tossing up dust and raising clouds—this is you."
People, do you still know where Yunfeng has landed? When the occasion arises, he presents himself face-to-face; when presented face-to-face, he acts with immediate decisiveness.
It is laughable that those who fight cocks do not even recognize a water buffalo.

Ascending the hall during the snow, a monk asked: "When Bodhidharma sat facing the wall at Shaolin for nine years and the Second Patriarch stood in the snow with it reaching his waist, what exactly was the matter?
The Master replied: "Rare are those who come with pierced ears; most are but men marking the water. The monk pressed further:
"The Second Patriarch said, 'My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to pacify my mind. What was the meaning of this? The Master replied: "A commotion!"

The Master said: "To transmute iron into gold and jade is easy; to exhort you to eliminate right and wrong is difficult. The monk then prostrated. The Master continued:
"The white ox stands revealed in the open field; Nanquan has no place to seek its tracks. The fragrant elephant crosses the river; Samantabhadra loses his realm.
Cold and piercing, the jade towers bristle with frost; pure and white, the silver seas bloom with flowers. Before the hall of the ancient Buddha..."
The lantern dances; the night-brightening screen stands outside. The dew-pillar intermingles, proclaiming the ancestral wind of Shaoshi and revealing the Buddha-dharma of the New Year.
The sun overflows the eyes; as ever, the waters are green and the mountains are blue. Spring returns to the great earth, until the rivers are clear and the seas are tranquil.
Striking the meditation seat: the rustic old man knows not the strength of Yao and Shun; beat the drum loudly to celebrate the abundance.

In the year [of the Master’s passing], on the occasion of the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "From the Deer Park at the beginning until the Bahudhaka River at the end, in this interval between the two, he never spoke a single word.
What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "A holeless iron hammer is hurled right in your face."
The student said, "What can be done about the entire Tripitaka? The Master said, "Recognize the meaning at the tip of the hook; do not mistake it for the fixed mark on the scale.
The student said, "White clouds may indeed come over the green peaks, but the bright moon cannot be made to descend from the blue sky. The Master said, "You are led astray.
The Master then said, "For forty-nine years and over three hundred assemblies, Śākyamuni Buddha was much like a phantom."
The Master said: "Illusion produces the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the grasses, trees, and forests; the cities, towns, and villages;
and all people, animals, plants, and wood—all of these do not contradict the true mark (*dharmatā*). Finally, he again creates an illusory tiger that returns to devour the illusionist.

Once the illusionist is extinguished, all illusions are extinguished along with him. When all illusions are extinguished, even the extinction of illusion is extinguished. After a long silence, he struck the meditation seat and said: "Dual..."
Beneath the forest trees, few people pass; before the Many-Sons Stūpa, the bustle is like a marketplace.

Entering the hall, he raised the following case: A monk asked Dongshan, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddha? Dongshan replied, "The nest knows the wind; the burrow knows the rain. The Master offered this verse:
"The nest knows the wind; the burrow knows the rain. This one clear phrase is raised for you: The myriad phenomena of the forested world..."
The elephants all mingle and intermingle; from Bohai and Silla, they dance and leap together in unison. Tell all people not to be so crude and reckless! As the ancient masters have said:
"That which precedes heaven is the progenitor of the mind."

[The Master] said, "Later, Mingzhao pointed it out for him; was he truly decisive or not? The Master said, "Looking over the precipice with eyes fixed on the riverbank—this is a groundless cause for grief.
The monk stepped forward and asked, "Today a student asks the Master: when the tree falls and the vines wither, where do the words return?
I wonder, Master, how will you instruct me? The Master gave a shout. The monk bowed. The Master then [continued]:
It is said: When Yunmen led his assembly to Fuyang to spend the summer retreat, he lost one of his "eyes. Xiyuan left Tianping behind;
they deliberated on two errors and did not spare even a few strands of their eyebrows. Yunfeng had years but no virtue, so he did not allow anyone to stay for the summer;
they deliberated on two errors, stirring up wind and raising grass, yet he did not lead his followers. Those from all quarters stayed for the summer, trailing water and mud.
He does not delve into the dragon palace; he does not wade across the vast ocean. He does not enter the tiger’s den; he topples Mount Sumeru.
He simply drinks water to quench his thirst and eats rice to relieve his hunger. When Zen travelers meet, they merely snap their fingers—how many can truly know this mind?
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The Venerable Xuefeng said: 'This plot of ground has been entrusted to all of you for a very long time.
You must know that this plot of ground is not produced from the seven treasures; it constantly emits immeasurable jewel-light day and night, and does not rely on the illumination of the sun and moon.
The Buddhas of the three periods have never trodden upon it, nor have the six generations of patriarchs.'"

The Master’s path does not reach there; even an enlightened monk cannot see it. You, the assembly here now, throughout the twenty-four hours of the day—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or in every movement of turning, bending, and stretching—if suddenly you stumble and step upon it, performing a somersault like a cartwheel, and awaken from that experience, only then will you know:
it has always been as level as a mirror; who said it was as rotten as mud?

On the first day of the seventh month, [the Master] ascended the hall while walking along the path. A monk asked, "What kind of person is it who leaves the Eastern Land in the morning and goes to the Western Heaven in the evening?
The Master said, "The Stone Brave-Heart at the crossroads. The monk pressed further, "Yesterday someone came from Tiantai."
"Why did you go to Mount Nanyue? The Master said, "A catfish climbing a bamboo pole. The student asked further, "There is one person who is always on the road, yet never leaves home;
there is another person who is always at home, yet never leaves the road. Tell me, which is superior and which is inferior?
The Master said, "Rabbits and horses have horns; oxen and sheep do not. The student asked, "If that is so, then [the one] before the courtyard..."
"A single leaf falls, and the whole world knows it is autumn. The Master said, "One who knows the time and discerns what is appropriate is fit to be a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend).
The monk bowed; the Master then said, "For thirty years I have lived at Zihu; my strength has been sustained by the morning gruel and evening meal.
With nothing to do, I go down the mountain for a stroll, asking those who meet me: 'Do you understand? Zihu is much like one whose heart is solitary despite his advanced age."
Yunfeng, however, was not like this: "For three or four years I have resided at this monastery; my strength remains robust from the morning and evening meals.
When we go down the mountain for communal labor, the fragrance of the ripening rice fills the ten-thousand-acre fields."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What was the meaning of Bodhidharma’s wall-gazing? The Master said, "Rancid rice and a clay tea stove.
The monk pressed further, "And what about the Sixth Patriarch treading the pestle? The Master said, "A rabbit eating cow's milk. The monk asked, "One person says he does not recognize it;
another says he does not understand. Where does the meaning lie? The Master said, "Fenglin says *tazhi*. The monk [remained silent].

After prostrating, the Master said: "Bodhidharma did not recognize [his own nature], yet sat facing the wall for nine years. The Sixth Patriarch did not understand, yet spent his life treading the rice-mortar.
This has brought trouble upon their descendants, who stumble here and there. It is like the daughter-in-law riding the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it;
or Zhang Gong drinking the wine while Li Gong gets drunk. Good brother!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Earth, water, fire, wind, space, awakening, and consciousness. Within a single mote of dust lies the true void;
from this all Tathāgatas of the three periods have emerged. It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. Who else could walk alone through the vast expanse?
From the crown of his head, he releases a falcon soaring toward the heavens."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "Last night during the small *paramita* (private instruction), the Master cited a monk’s question to Touzi:
'When a person who has died the great death comes back to life, what then? Touzi replied: 'Night travel is not permitted; one must arrive by dawn. What is the meaning of this? The Master said:
"Before and after the winter solstice, sand flies and stones run. The monk pressed further: "Master Zhengtang’s verse says: 'I have doubted for a thousand..."
The azure jade essence of a thousand years has transformed into a single piece of autumn-water bone.
The Sea God wished to protect it but could not; one night, the head of the giant turtle suddenly lifted it up. I do not know, Reverend Zhengtang, what kind of eyes you possess.
The Master said: "One must quickly turn one's eyes to look at the immortal; do not look at the fan in the immortal's hand. He further asked: "As for the verse you composed, Reverend, it says:"
"When the yang energy arises, there is no hard ground. During the Qin dynasty, flowers grew from the drill-holes of the *chalu* carriage.
The tongue of the ancient Buddha of Huaixi has no bone; he chews the void thoroughly and spits out peaches. "It does not hinder him from walking hand-in-hand with Touzi.
The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, have never spoken such words. Do not slander me! The student replied, "This disciple is at fault," and prostrated himself. The Master then—
It is said: "A song from Yunmen on the twenty-fifth of the twelfth lunar month; a song from Yunfeng on the twenty-fifth of the mid-winter month.
When the *jiā* tube moves and the flying ash stirs, the sun’s orb is exactly at its zenith.
Last night, the carp of the Eastern Sea swallowed the fierce tiger of the Southern Mountain, startling Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra until they fled into the pillar before the hall. He lets out a shout.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "Regarding the Buddha-dharma at the beginning of the New Year, Jingqing said it 'exists,' while Mingjiao said it 'does not exist.
I wonder, what was the intent of these ancients? The Master said: "A pair of unperforated iron hammers. The monk stepped forward and said: "I, this student, ask the Master."
"At the beginning of the New Year, is there even any Buddha-dharma? I wonder, Master, how will you instruct us?
The Master replied, "The pillar blossoms; the lantern bears fruit. The monk then bowed. The Master then said, "The planning for a year depends on spring."
The plan for a single day lies in the Tiger (Yin). In the first month, the Tiger is established; the first day of the year falls under the Tiger.
As the New Year begins its reign, all things are renewed: the Sangha hall is new, the beds and bedding are new, and the food, drink, and medicinal decoctions are new.

Within this one hall, the Chan monks are like phoenixes and qilin; each one holds the treasure of the numinous serpent, and every person harbors the jewel of the vast ocean. But tell me: what of the Buddha?
"Does the Dharma have new and old?—*Hah!*"—with this shout, he invites the head monks to the hall.
"Excellent!"—three strikes of the board. "All you kinsmen, come and investigate. Since you already well know the proper timing, [enter].
"I shall not repeat it a third time. When the ancients spoke thus, it was much like pressing a cow's head down to make it eat grass.

Yunfeng, however, does not do so. "Excellent! Strike the board three times; draw up your feet and mount the meditation cushion. With a backbone forged of cast iron, pass through the Patriarch’s Barrier.
In a single breath, turn over the entire Great Canon. Turn your back and pick up Mount Sumeru. Seven places where the mind is sought..."
There is no mind to be sought; the eight returns distinguish the seeing, yet there is no seeing to be returned. One has entered a celestial palace in a dream and remains unawakened;
the golden cock crows atop the jade balustrade.
While returning from his travels to give a formal lecture in the Dharma Hall, a monk asked: "In the past, Master Bao sent someone to deliver a message to Great Master Si:
'Why do you not go down the mountain to teach and transform sentient beings? Why do you always gaze at the clouds and sky? What was the meaning of this? The Master said:

"The clouds on the ridge peak have no leisure; the water flowing down the ravine is far too busy. The monk pressed further: "What about the Way of Si? The Master said: "He has been sitting for eighty years."
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time have all been swallowed by me in a single gulp. What sentient beings are there left to transform?
Tell me, what kind of eyes does Sita possess? The Master said, "His garrulous tongue extends three thousand li.

The student asked, "When you, Master, go down the mountain to teach and transform sentient beings, are you the same as or different from the ancients? The Master said, "Always on the road, never departing."
The assembly prostrated. The Master then said: "Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell; where there is no Buddha, pass by quickly.
Even three thousand miles away, do not mistakenly mention [this] to anyone you meet. The old man Zhaozhou was much like one who embraces a bridge pillar while bathing.
I cast off the mooring ropes and set sail. Since my departure, more than forty days have passed. Where there is a Buddha, I have shattered his divination charts with a awl;

where there is no Buddha, I have likewise examined and traversed those places. I have traveled through three prefectures and five counties, and whenever I encountered people, I have tested them by posing a wrong question.
Yet, the land is vast and the people sparse; those who truly understand are few. Plucking the willow blossoms—plucking the willow blossoms. Suddenly, the green mountains...
Remembering this, he returned home. Thinking he must see the dusty world again, he came back down.

He ascended the hall and said: "The nature of awareness is wondrously luminous; original awareness is luminously wondrous. This cuts off the life-root of the patch-robed monks and clears away the single aperture of the ultimate path.
A cowhide drum covers the pillar; the pillar shrieks and squeals. Those with ordinary ears do not hear it; the various sages rebuke them."
A laugh of derision. The void leaps and dances through the three stages. An iron cauldron brews tea, not unlike a small pot.
Magu and Xitang ascend to the high seat. A monk asked: "Duan Lizi said: 'The village lion is performed in the village.'"
The eyebrows and eyelashes move all at once; when the mouth opens, it is nothing but a blunt, straightforward thing. There is no need for anyone to offer service or honor.
Even if one were to perform such antics before an emperor, it would still be nothing more than a hollow, empty clamor. What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "A true lion cub;
he knows how to roar the lion's roar. The student asked: "But what about a tiny gnat? Suppose it were to act upon the eyelashes of a mosquito—"
Kuo went out to the crossroads and cried out: "The land is vast and the people are few; those who meet one another are rare. Moreover, what of it?
The monk said, "I have never seen such a strange sentient being. The monk bowed. The Master then said:
"Awakening the thousand-year-old dream of Mātaṅga, summoning back the single sail of the Boatman—how does this compare to sitting in meditative poise within the lion’s den and letting forth a roar?"
A single sound empties heaven and earth; the thirteenfold ocean of the Flower Treasury is entirely contained within a single speck of dust.
If one’s spiritual mechanism can achieve solitary liberation, behold how it is naturally resonant from all eight sides.
The Master ascends the hall for the Bathing of the Buddha ceremony. A monk asks: "The body of the pure dharma-realm fundamentally has no appearing or disappearing;
yet, through the power of great compassionate vows, it manifests coming and going. I venture to ask: by whose grace and power did Prince Siddhārtha receive his realization?

The Master says: "A patch-robed monk’s staff. The monk steps forward and asks: "I do not know what excellence this staff possesses. The Master says: "It helps one cross the waters of the broken bridge, and accompanies one back to the light."
Geyun asked, "Ultimately, are Prince Siddhārtha and the monk’s staff one or two? The Master said, "Three feet, one zhang, six chi.
Now, let us join hands and go home together. The monk bowed. The Master then said: "Throughout heaven and earth, none equal the Buddha;
In the worlds of the ten directions, there is no peer. Whatever exists in the world, I have seen it all— One..."

"There is absolutely no one like the Buddha; this is Śākyamuni Bhagavān. By standing on one foot for twenty-one days and chanting verses in praise of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he surpassed Maitreya by ninety-one *kalpas*. When one examines this, what a truly great man he is!
Is there anyone present here today who can surpass Maitreya and exceed Śākyamuni? If there were such a person, they too would deserve thirty blows. He turned around.
