[The others] came to know [of this]. When King Aśoka heard of it, he came out and said, "You two, why all this 'zhi-hu-ze-er' (pedantic talk)?
If it were not for my Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s true-body relic stūpa, even with such supernatural powers and wondrous functions, there would be no place to exercise them.
The three clapped their hands and laughed loudly, "He-he! Now tell me, what was it they laughed at? On a quiet night...
When the water is cold, the fish do not feed; with a boat full of moonlight, they return home.
Entering the hall, he said: "The scriptures state: 'All obstacles are ultimate enlightenment; whether mindfulness is attained or lost, there is nothing that is not liberation;
whether dharmas are established or destroyed, all are called nirvana; whether wisdom or folly, both are collectively prajñā. [He] held up his staff and said: 'Night...'"
Half-releasing the black chicken, he startled the Brahma King from his sleep.
Then he descended from his seat and ascended the hall: "A fragrant breeze comes from the south; the halls and pavilions grow cool. Old Miaoxi has mistaken this for a donkey's saddle bridge.
Acting as a father’s chin, you bring so many people down with you. Speculating about this matter—do you know where all the Buddhas emerge?
The Yellow River clears itself only once every three thousand years. (He plants his staff upright and descends from the seat.)
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an ancient case: A monk asked Guizong, “What is the Buddha? Guizong said, “I do not refuse to tell you, but I fear you will not believe me.
The monk said, “If the Master speaks with such sincerity, how would I dare not believe? Guizong said, “You yourself are it.”
The monk asked, "How does one maintain this? Zong said, "A single film in the eye causes empty flowers to fall in confusion. The verse says: "A three-foot sword for the sake of the state’s security;
Five-character poems are the ladder to heaven. If there is a path to the blue sky, one must reach its end;
If one's name is not upon the golden scroll, one vows never to return."

For the practitioner, there is the blessing of descending into fire; there are good fortune and misfortune, regret and shame; there are formation, abiding, decay, and emptiness; there is finding life within death;
there is girding oneself with stones to grind grain; there is the cricket in the fire; and there is swallowing the tiger whole.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is the Way? Zhaozhou said, “The one outside the wall.
The monk said, “I am not asking about that Way. Zhaozhou said, “Which Way are you asking about? The monk said, “I am asking about the Great Way. Zhaozhou said, “The Great Way penetrates Chang’an.
The verse says: The Great Way penetrates Chang’an; Throughout antiquity and today, none have traveled it to its end. It is like a catfish climbing a bamboo pole.
The tiger watches the water-mill; he pushes out the horse-winnowing basket of Jiangxi. He kicks over the broken stove of Songshan.
Entering the hall, he says: "Hastening at dawn, hastening at dusk; the alms bowl opens its mouth, seeking only to devour the void. Nanquan smashed the cauldron;
Ganji prostrated before the steamer. Striking the whisk, he says: "Ten thousand miles, the eighth and ninth months; a single body, northwest."

Wind. On the anniversary of the First Patriarch’s passing, he offered incense: "Crossing waters, he met a sheep; traveling through Wei and visiting Liang, he sat coldly for eight or nine years, utterly without a clue.
Three or five times he was poisoned—how truly distressing! If you say he came ten thousand *li* from the West to transmit [the Dharma]..."
The Buddha’s Mind-Seal: A man without nostrils—what with which shall he smell the fragrance?
For the sake of the Abbot Hua, I extinguish the funeral pyre; I topple the City of Nirvana and shatter the Kingdom of Huaxu.
Yangqi’s donkey leaps about until heaven and earth grow narrow; atop the mountain of the five aggregates, the firelight flashes and blazes.
Ascending the hall: On this day of the beginning of spring, all things are most auspicious. Peach talismans are nailed upon the gates; at the hedges, the pi-li flute is blown.

As for those who study the profound under the forest trees, they have mouths that hang only on the wall. When the clay ox is whipped to hasten the spring plowing, its entire body is revealed as nothing but golden bone.

Ascending the hall on the Lantern Festival, a monk asked, "This Dharma-gate of mine is called the 'Inexhaustible Lamp. It illuminates all that is dark, and its light never ends. What is this Inexhaustible Lamp?
The Master said, "The sun rises at the edge of the sky; the moon descends. Before the railing, the mountains are deep and the waters cold.
The monk further asked, "Do you permit a student to continue the flame and link the fragrance [of the lineage]? The Master said, "Do not engage in deluded thoughts. The monk bowed.
[The Master] gave a shout and returned to the assembly. The Master said, "What limit is there to this fellow playing with lumps of mud?

He then continued: "Today is the fifteenth of the first month; everywhere in the villages there is singing and dancing. Upon the curved wooden seat, this old monk speaks of Buddhas and Patriarchs as best he can.
Xuefeng rolls the ball; Heyshan beats the drum. Startled, the carp of the Eastern Sea swallows up the South... [He left the sentence unfinished.]
The mountain tiger warns all people: do not be reckless! I have seen that the lamp-lighting Buddha’s original radiance and auspicious signs were like this.
[He] ascends the hall and cites Master Fayan’s instruction to the assembly: "If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the conditions of time and season.
The ancients possessed no small amount of skillful means. Have you not seen how Master Shitou, while reading the *Zhao Lun*, said: "To comprehend the myriad..."
"Only the Sage can truly take all things as himself. Other teachers say, "The Sage has no self; there is nothing that is not his own.
He has a saying which he calls the *Cantong qi* (Mysterious Agreement). At its conclusion, it says: "The mind of the Great Immortal of India does not exceed these words.
Yet throughout the middle sections, he speaks merely according to the occasion. [The Master] comments: "If one were to truly bring this forth, the [mind of the] Indian..."

Even the mind of the Great Immortal Tu cannot contain this single phrase. If you all wish to understand that the Sage has no self, yet there is nowhere he does not manifest as self, go and ask the pillar.
Small Assembly for Disciples. Compiled by Baosheng and Wenzao.
Layou pointed out the five illnesses; Xiyuan deliberated upon the two errors. A well-frog is not fit to discuss this.
The Eastern Sea. One cannot speak of ice and frost to an insect of summer. If you are a swift falcon soaring through the void, you ought to seize the opportune moment;
if you are a fish exhausted in a shallow pool, your splashing against the waves is but toil in vain.

Therefore, from the ancient Buddhas and Patriarchs down to the elder monks of the world, there are none who did not attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment upon mountains of knives and swords, amidst cauldrons of boiling water and furnace coals, thereby delivering and rescuing all beings.
Sentient beings—if I, this mountain monk, look at them, they are like a weight dipped in vinegar. (He lets out a shout.
At the end of summer retreat, as autumn begins, you brothers go east and west;
it is like a strong man extending his arm, requiring no outside force, or like a lion roaming, seeking no companion. This is because beneath everyone’s feet there is a... (He lets out another shout.)
This is the living path that penetrates to the heavens. The Buddhas of the three periods, the six generations of patriarchs, and the old monks of the world walk hand-in-hand with you.
Have you not seen how Master Yunmen asked Dongshan, "Where have you recently come from? "Chadu," he replied. "Where did you spend the summer retreat?
"At Baoci in Hunan. "When did you leave there? "On the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month. Yunmen said, "Let go!"
"You shall receive three blows of the staff. The next day, [the monk] went to the abbot's quarters and asked, "Yesterday I was granted three blows of the staff by the Master;
I do not know where my fault lay. Yunmen said, "You rice-bag! From Jiangxi to Hunan, everyone goes about like this."
Dongshan attained great enlightenment beneath these words. Yunmen drew forth his sky-reaching long sword; its formidable, divine edge was not easily met.
Dongshan dared to charge at that white blade with his bare body. At such a moment, what is it like? The golden crow pecks through the crystal shell;
the jade hare pushes open the gates of the azure sea.
New Year’s Eve. I, the idle man of the Way who has severed all learning and attained non-action, simply counts thirty-six decans as one year.
I do not fear birth, death, or old age; let the "thirtieth day of the twelfth month" come as it may. Like a bell suspended on its frame, I wait for the strike before I ring.
Like a mirror set upon its stand, I reflect whatever object comes before me. This old monk’s destiny lies in the hexagram *Kan* (the abyss); the spirit of poverty mocks me.

The bag has no silk-thread for binding ants; the kitchen is cut off from the crumbs that gather flies. Speaking in every dust mote, speaking in every land, speaking with blazing intensity—there is not a single dharma that can be spoken.
Inner emptiness, outer emptiness, ultimate emptiness—all are empty. The cold forest is frozen and locked; the wooden Buddha of the vermilion clouds is burned to ashes.
When the spring returns and the laws of warmth prevail, the iron ox of Shanzhou is awakened; amidst a throng of ten thousand people, he is driven forth.
The *nà* exorcism. At the head of the hundred theatrical performances, the *kūlěi* puppets are pulled. In the end, what kind of business has this accomplished? (He strikes the whisk.
Meeting [him] yet not encountering the hand that seasons the soup, the plum blossoms are betrayed once again for another year.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Yuejiang, Volume One;
The Recorded Sayings of Master Yuejiang, Volume Two: Comments on Ancient Cases (Nianggu).
Compiled by the disciple Zu’an, Abbot of Huiri Chan Temple in Wenzhou Prefecture.
Recorded is Deshan’s address to the assembly: “Tonight, I shall not answer any questions. Anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows.
At that time, a monk came forward and bowed. Deshan struck him immediately. The monk said, “I have not even asked a question. Deshan replied, “Where have you come from?”
A man asked, "What country is he from? Deshan replied, "He is a man from Silla. Xuefeng said, "Before he has even stepped onto the ship's railing, thirty blows would have been well-deserved.
Fayan said, "Master Deshan of great stature has split his own discourse into two pieces. Yuanming said, "Master Deshan of great stature has the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake.
Xuedou said, "The two elders were ill; though they were skilled at cutting the long to patch the short and discarding the heavy for the light, one still cannot see Deshan."
"Not yet possible. Why? Master Deshan seems to have grasped the authority over the outer gates; he lacks the sword that brings no chaos by failing to sever what must be severed.
Do you all wish to recognize this monk from Silla? He is merely a blind fellow who has run straight into a pillar."
The Master said: "Old Hanshi [Deshan] had a single white staff; he would strike even if a Buddha came, and he would strike even if a Patriarch came.
Yet, in an ordinary moment, it was snapped in two by a monk from Silla. Fayen Yuanming each extended a hand, but they could only save half of it.
Xuedou said: "If you wish to recognize the Silla monk, he was simply one who ran straight into a pillar."
"Blind fellow! You increase his majestic brilliance by so much. Is there anyone who can act as the true master for Deshan?
He raised the case: One day Xuefeng was performing communal labor; carrying a bundle of rattan himself, he encountered a monk on the road, whereupon Xuefeng simply dropped it down.

Just as the monk was about to pick it up, Xuefeng stepped on him and knocked him over. Upon returning, he recounted the incident to Changsheng, saying, "I have been quite swift in stepping on that monk today.
Changsheng said, "Only then will you truly have entered the Nirvana Hall on behalf of that monk. Xuefeng then desisted.
Xuedou remarked, "Changsheng is much like a neighbor from the west who offers condolences when a member of the eastern family has died; he too deserves a kick."
The Master said: "Xuefeng greedily gazed at the moon in the sky and lost the oar in his hand; Changsheng borrowed another's hand to perform a fist-punch;
Xuedou poured oil to save the fire—these are all cases of drawing one's bow after the thief has fled."
To cite the story of Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu: while standing in attendance, Mazu looked with his eyes at the whisk in the corner of the meditation seat.
Baizhang said, "Using it right here, yet detached from using it. Mazu asked, "After this, when you open your two flaps of skin [to preach], with what will you save people?
Baizhang took up the whisk and held it upright. Mazu said, "Using it right here, yet detached from using it. Baizhang then hung the whisk back on its stand.
At the old site, Baizhang simply shouted, and Baizhang remained deaf for three days straight. Xuedou said: "How strange!

O Zen adepts, nowadays there are many who list his lineage, but those who investigate its source are extremely few. Everyone says that Baizhang attained great enlightenment under that shout; yet is this truly so?
Nevertheless, 'diao' and 'dao' may look similar, but 'yu' and 'lu' differ. If one is truly clear..."
O blind men! You cannot deceive others by even a single point. Just as Mazu said, "After you have opened those two flaps of skin [your mouth], with what will you act as a person?
Baizhang then held up his whisk. Was this like an insect boring into wood? Or was it like the simultaneous pecking and hatching?
If you wish to understand why everyone’s ears were deaf for three days, know that refined gold from a great furnace remains unchanged in its color.
The Master said: "The lion teaches its cubs; this is the secret instruction for deluding them. Mazu had it; Baizhang was left with three days of deafness.
Fine food is not for a satiated person to eat. Xuedou said: "Refined gold from a great furnace should not change its color;
one ought to give him a shout."
Chongshou raised his finger at a stool and said, "If you recognize this stool, it exceeds its surroundings.
Yunmen said, "If you recognize this stool, heaven and earth are vastly different. Xuedou said, "A vast marsh conceals mountains; a principle can subdue a leopard."
The Master said: "Xuedou speaks thus, yet he still does not recognize the bench.
He then cited the Great Master Yongjia, who went to the Sixth Patriarch, circumambulated the meditation seat three times, struck his staff once, and stood there with solemn composure.
The Patriarch asked, "A śramaṇa possesses three thousand dignified manners and eighty thousand subtle practices. From what direction have you come, Venerable One?"

[He] came forward. [Huineng] gave rise to great conceit. Xuedou then shouted, saying: "If he had let out that one shout at that moment, we would have avoided seeing this case of a dragon's head and a snake's tail.
He then raised the case again: [The Sixth Patriarch] circumambulated the meditation seat three times, struck his staff once, and stood there upright.
On behalf of the Patriarch, Xuedou said: "Before you reached Caoxi, I would have given you thirty blows!"
The Master said: "An honored guest from Yongjia’s Longmen Gate; the East Pavilion of the Sixth Patriarch stands wide open.
A once-in-a-thousand-year moment; wind and clouds meet in harmony. Xuedou, acting on behalf of Yongjia, let out a shout. He then acted on behalf of the Patriarch, saying:
"Before you have even reached Caoxi, I shall give you thirty blows! This is truly extraordinary. But tell me, did these two great elders [attain the truth]?
Ganmo. [The Master] cites Yangshan, who pointed to a snow lion and asked, "Is there anyone who can pass through this color?
Yunmen said, "At that moment, he should have pushed it over. Xuedou said, "He only knew how to push it over; he did not know how to lift it up."
The Master said: "Yunmen pushed him over; Xuedou helped him up. To truly see Yangshan, one must still reckon thirty li short.
He then cited Xiangyan’s hanging word: "It is like a man climbing a tree, holding a branch in his mouth with neither hand nor foot grasping a branch.
If someone beneath the tree asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey, if he does not answer, he violates the questioner's intent; yet if he answers..."
"One loses one's body and forfeits one's life. At such a time, what is it? There was a Venerable Head-Tiger who said, "I do not ask about having climbed the tree;
please, Master, speak before climbing it. Yanguan laughed heartily. Xuedou said, "To speak from atop the tree is easy;
to speak beneath the tree is difficult. When I climb the tree, bring me a question as well!"
The Master said: "Xiangyan held fast to the secure barrier, allowing not even a drop of water to pass through.
Had it not been for the emergence of Head Seat Houtou, how could this discourse have been transmitted for a thousand ages? I, Yuyang, dare ask Xuedou: 'The Master has already climbed the tree;
I only fear he cannot descend.'"
A monk asked Luzu, "What is 'speaking without speaking'? Luzu said, "Where is your mouth? The monk said, "I have no mouth.
Luzu said, "Then with what do you eat your rice? The monk was speechless. Xuedou said, "He should have been struck across the back with a staff!
Such a fellow cannot close his mouth once it has opened, nor can he open it once it has closed."
The Master said: "This monk is like a snake that has its head in a cage but its tail trailing outside. At that time, had he been asked, 'With what do you eat?
he should have simply replied, 'He is not hungry; what would he eat? When it comes to this point, even the Elder Xuedou would have no place to wield his staff."

A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? Feng said, "Staring with wide eyes, one cannot see the bottom. The monk asked, "And what of those who drink from it?
Feng said, "It does not enter through the mouth. The monk took this up with Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "It cannot enter through the nostrils either.
The monk then asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? Zhaozhou said, "Bitter."
The monk asked, "What about one who drinks? Zhaozhou said, "Dead. When Xuefeng heard this being cited, he remarked, "Zhaozhou is an ancient Buddha;

from this point on, he would no longer answer questions. Xuedou said, "Everyone in the assembly says that Xuefeng did not bring up the monk’s question, and that is why Zhaozhou refused to acknowledge him.
To interpret the matter in such a way deeply wrongs the ancients. Xuedou does not think so; he would simply chop the nails and cut the bolts."
Iron. A master of the fundamental division who levels the high by means of the low is difficult to emulate.

The Master said, "To bore through tortoise shells and strike at roof tiles; to stir up the turbid and exalt the clear; to cut off the tongues of all people under heaven—Xuedou is not without this ability.
Yet, for all his skill, he still does not know where the ancients met. Do you know where Xuefeng and Zhaozhou met? You have attained it."
One person gave a cow back; another returned a horse.
A monk asked West Hall Master: "When there is a question and an answer, the roles of guest and host are clearly defined. But when there is neither question nor answer, what then?
The Master said: "I am afraid it would rot away. A monk asked Changqing: "When there is a question and an answer, the roles of guest and host are clearly defined..."
"But when there is neither question nor answer, what then? Jing said, "Everyone says upon meeting that they have retired from office;
yet, who has ever seen a single person beneath the forest trees? Xuedou said, "Why not give him his proper fodder?"
The Master said: "One person cuts off the flow of all streams; one person follows the waves and drifts with the current; one person encompasses heaven and earth.
When there is a question, there is an answer from Yuyang, and the roles of host and guest are clearly distinct. But when there is neither question nor answer, what then?
He simply says: "Host and guest are clearly distinct. This is to avoid seeing this monk running south and rushing north.
Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "At my late teacher’s place, I received sixty blows three times, which were like being brushed with a bundle of mugwort.
Now I am thinking of having one more blow; who will step forward to deal it? A monk came forth from the assembly and said, "I will deal it.
Linji handed his staff to the monk; as the monk was about to take it, Linji struck him. Xuedou said: "This is where Linji lets go."
This is more dangerous. He brought it back too quickly.
The Master said, "Linji is much like a poor man thinking of his old debts. It is a pity he let him off then.
Had I waited for him to raise his staff, I would have overturned the meditation seat. Linji would surely have had to settle the matter under the bright window. (Xuedou)
Dòu said: "To let it go is perilous; to pull it back in too quickly. A cangue upon the head and shackles upon the feet.
He cited an occasion when Qinshan went up into the hall one day, raised his fist, and then opened his hand, saying, "When opened, it becomes a palm, with the five fingers distinct from one another.
He then closed his hand again, saying, "Now it is a fist; surely there is no longer high or low. "Is there still any room for deliberation? A monk [stepped forward].
He stepped out from the assembly and raised his fist. Yanshou said, "You are merely a fellow who knows nothing of opening and closing. Xuedou said, "Xuedou does not think so.
He then raised his fist and said, "When clenched, it is a fist; there is high and low. He then opened his hand and said, "When opened, it becomes a palm;
there is no factionalism and no partiality. Now tell me: is it better to benefit others by letting go, or is it better to benefit others by holding fast? Open!

Building a carriage. Grasping the handle, one’s tracks meet those of others. If you say, "I build my carriage inside my door, yet when I go out, my tracks meet with others," I know that you are making your living inside a ghost cave.
The Master said: "Qinshan opens up a world within the pores of a lotus fiber; Xuedou is accustomed to playing on the swings atop a tiger’s tongue.
Examining them closely, neither can shut the mouths of those from all quarters. I, however, am not like this."
He then raised his fist and said, "The Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all the old monks of the world—all beg for their lives right here.

He then opened his hand and continued, "It reaches the point where Mount Sumeru towers precipitously, the waters of the sea surge into waves, and throughout the ten directions the wind whistles. Suddenly, there is a man who comes forth and says, 'Venerable Monk, even so!'"
He was simply a man of no opening or closing; yet, one must grant him that he possessed the "single eye.
A monk asked Muzhou, "What is it like when one bows high to Śākyamuni but does not pay homage to Maitreya?
Muzhou said, "Yesterday someone asked this; I chased them out. The monk said, "I fear, Master, that I am not being sincere. Muzhou said, "The staff!"
"He is not here. [Muzhou] offered the handle of his broom for thirty coins. Xuedou said: "Muzhou had only the heart to accept the jade tablet, but lacked the intention to cede the city walls."
The Master said: "If one climbs a mountain but does not reach the summit, one will not know the vastness of the universe.

If one enters the sea but does not reach the bottom, one will not know the depth of the blue ocean. This monk let loose three parts of his soft-headed stubbornness, and thus the private property of Muzhou was entirely exhausted at once.
Xuedou’s critique in this manner is truly like a rabbit eating cow’s milk.
Zhaozhou raised a jujube tree and asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "From the land of Han.

Zhaozhou said, "In the land of Han, does the Son of Heaven still hold the Buddha-dharma in high regard? The monk said, "What a pity! Fortunately it was I whom you questioned; had you questioned someone else, disaster would have ensued.
Zhaozhou asked, "Why would that be? The monk replied, "People do not even recognize him; what Buddha-dharma could there be to hold in high regard?"
Zhushu asked, "Venerable, how many years have you been ordained? The monk replied, "Twenty summer retreats. Zhushu said, "Excellent!
Yet I see no one here," and he struck him. Xuedou said, "This monk deserved the blow; however, once gone, he will not return.
Although Zhushu’s command was carried out, alas, he stirred up waves where there was no wind."

The Master said: "This monk did not come from the land of Han. Had he truly come from the land of Han, even if there were a staff on the jujube tree, I still would not have been able to strike him. He is simply a man with no foothold.
How is this known? Have you not seen Xuedou say: 'Once gone, he does not return'?"
[The Master] cited the story of Zhaozhou asking an old woman, "Where are you going? The woman said, "I am going to steal Zhaozhou’s bamboo shoots.
Zhaozhou said, "What will you do when you encounter Zhaozhou? The woman then gave him a slap, and Zhaozhou simply stopped there. Xuedou said, "A good slap! But give her two more slaps;
even then, there would be no place for examination."
The Master said: "Zhaozhou stops; the old woman exerts herself but gains no merit. To strike her two more times is also the perspective of an old woman.
He then cited the day Baoshou opened the hall when Sansheng pushed forward a monk; Baoshou struck him immediately. Sansheng said, "Acting like this..."
"Person! You have blinded the eyes of the entire city of Zhenzhou! Having said this, Baoshou returned to his quarters. Xuedou said:
"Although Baoshou and Sansheng revealed the treasury of the true Dharma-eye of Linji, they only knew how to claim supremacy where there is no Buddha.
At that time, if that monk had been a man of substance, as soon as he was pushed out, he would have overturned the meditation seat. Even if..."
Baoshou’s full-functioning [action] still falls short by three thousand li.
The Master said: "Baoshou saw the rabbit and released the hawk; Sansheng pointed at the deer and called it a horse. They extinguished the Linji school."
These two old fellows—though Xuedou possesses eyes that settle heaven and earth and the skill to capture tigers and rhinoceroses, he did not realize the arrow had already passed to Silla;
instead, he waited for it in the Great Tang.
A monk asked Wuye, “What is the Buddha? Wuye said, “Do not engage in false conceptualization. Xuedou said, “He blocks the nostrils.
Another monk asked Mazu, “What is the Buddha? Mazu said, “The very mind is the Buddha. Xuedou said, “He props up the tongue.”
The Master said: "Xuedou’s nostrils lack half; his tongue does not emerge from his mouth.
If he wishes to meet the two great elders Wuye and Mazu, it will take sixty kalpas over three lifetimes."
A monk asked Deshan, "Where have all the sages of the past gone? Deshan said, "What? What?
The monk said, "When the imperial decree summons the flying dragon horse, the lame tortoise sticks its head out. Deshan then stopped speaking.

On the following day, after Deshan had finished his bath, the monk passed him tea. Deshan gave the monk a slap on the back, and the monk said, "Only now does this old fellow finally show some awareness."
Deshan said, "Even if refined gold has been smelted a hundred times, it must still be placed under the hammer of its own fundamental nature.

Since Deshan himself obstructed others with his own views, this monk was likewise subjected to humiliation. [The Master] took his staff, drew a line, and said, "Setting aside the case just now for a moment, where have all the sages of the past gone? As the assembly hesitated, he drove them away all at once.
The Master said: "Deshan was weak when encountering the strong, yet noble when meeting the lowly. This monk probed deep into the tiger’s den;
he nearly lost his body and his life. Xuedou also wishes to enter this protective community, yet he cannot avoid the laughter of bystanders."
Someone asked Emperor Yuzhang, "Where have all the sages of antiquity gone? The Emperor replied to him simply, "A bamboo platform with eight prongs.
Once, while Baofu was picking melons, Senior Monk Fu from Taiyuan arrived. Baofu said, "If you can speak, I will give you a melon."
Chi said, "Hand it over. Fu gave him a slice of melon. Chi took it and departed.
Xuedou said, "Though it was a dead snake, he knew how to handle it so it became alive. Who is a master of hand? Try to discern this for me."
The Master said: "Venerable Fu, it is like an insect boring through wood; by chance, it forms characters. Xuedou could not restrain his impatience and merely boasts of being a skilled hand.
Do you understand? A sweet melon is sweet from stem to tip; a bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip."
Nanquan addressed the assembly, saying, "The Way is not outside of things; that which is outside of things is not the Way. Zhaozhou came forward and asked, "What is the Way outside of things?
Nanquan struck him. Zhaozhou said, "Master, do not strike me; you might strike the wrong person in the future. Nanquan said, "Dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish;
it is the patch-robed monks who are difficult to deceive. Xuedou said, "Zhaozhou was like a dragon without..."
The "Horned" [creature] resembles a snake but has feet. At that time, regardless of whether the law is fully applied or there is no people, one must simply be caned and driven out.
The Master said: "Nanquan’s front end would frighten people to death; his back end would make people laugh to death. Xuedou said:
"Regardless of whether the law is fully applied or there is no people, one must simply be caned and driven out"—this saves half of it.
[The Master] cites Dongshan’s visit to Yunmen. Yunmen asked, "Where have you recently departed from? Dongshan said, "Chadu. Yunmen asked, "Where were you during the summer retreat?
Dongshan said, "Baoci in Hunan. Yunmen asked, "When did you leave? Dongshan said, "Last year, in the eighth month. Yunmen said: [and continued].
"I spare you three blows of the staff. On the following day, Xuefeng went up to inquire after him, saying, "Yesterday I was granted three blows of the staff by the Master;
I do not know where my fault lay. Yunmen said, "You rice-bag! In Jiangxi and Hunan, people go about exactly like this.
At these words, Xuefeng attained great enlightenment. Xuedou said, "Yunmen’s spirit was like that of a king; when pressed, he struck like ice."
It was dispersed and dissolved like salt in water. Had he acted according to the command at that time, his descendants would not have been cut off.
The Master said: "Yunmen may truly be said to possess a single grain of elixir that transforms iron into gold;
with a single word of ultimate truth, he turns the ordinary into the holy. Xuedou said: "Had he acted according to the command, his descendants would not have been cut off either."
It is well said that the principle is sound. Take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Consider one monk who went to visit Master Madaishi. The Master drew a circle and said, "If you enter, I will strike you;
if you do not enter, I will strike you. The monk entered, and the Master struck him. The monk said, "Master, you may not strike me. The Master leaned against [the wall].
[The Master] set down his staff and desisted. Xuedou said: "Both [cases] are incomplete. The Master may not strike me; I lean my staff against [him].
If he hesitates even for a moment, I shall strike him across the spine."
The Master said: "This monk has advanced and does not retreat; Master Ma has deployed and does not withdraw. This monk possesses the mechanism of biting the arrowhead;
Master Ma employs the tactic of the blunt blade. Although Xuedou wishes to carry out his commands to the full, he is still thirty li behind Great Master Ma."
Xinghua raised up the case of his questioning of the Rector Kebin: "Before long, you shall become a master who proclaims the Way. Kebin replied, "I will not enter your community.
Xinghua asked, "Do you enter it because you understand, or do you not enter it because you do not understand? Kebin said, "There is no connection between us.

Xinghua then struck him and said, "Rector Kebin, you have been defeated in the battle of Dharma; pay a fine of five strings of cash to provide a meal of 'drilling' (punishment). This concludes the account.
The next day at the time of the midday meal, Xinghua himself struck the gavel and said, "Venerable Kebin, you have not been victorious in the Dharma-battle;
you shall not eat. He then immediately drove him out. Xuedou said: "Kebin wished to inherit Xinghua’s lineage.
Let the fine and the expulsion from the monastery be for now, but he must first receive that one blow of the staff. Now, ask all of you: since the staff has already been taken, [what else remains?]"
"How do you seek it? Xuedou, wishing to settle this matter of injustice, said, "Tonight I shall clear the grievance for Kebin, the Rector," and with his staff, he struck them all down at once.
The Master said: "Regarding this koan, many have offered critiques throughout the ages.
Yet even for Xuedou, who was a master’s forge, he ultimately did not know where Xinghua’s tongue fell.
You must understand that this portion of rice is not for consumption unless one is Vekan, the Rector. Even if every person in the entire world were to come here,"
One dares not look directly at it with one's eyes.
[The Master] raised a case: A monk asked Changqing, "When many hands sift through gold, who is the one who obtains it? Changqing said, "Those with skillful means obtain it."
The monk asked, "Can a student still attain it? Jingqing said, "It is very far away. Xuedou, acting on behalf of that monk, would have shouted at that moment.
He further said: "If one has skillful means, one attains it; this is handed over with one hand. If one lacks skillful means, one does not attain it;
this is handed over with both hands. Can a student still attain it? Heaven! Heaven!"
The Master said: "At Yuwang, it was not so. When many hands sift gold, who is the one that finds it? [The Master] struck him across the back with his staff;
not only did he sever this monk’s life-root, but he also spared Xuedou from later dragging through the mud and water."
Daci raised the matter of Great Compassion to the assembly, saying, "I, this mountain monk, do not know how to answer questions; I simply recognize the illness.
At that time, a monk stepped forward, and Daci immediately returned to his quarters. Xuedou said, "In general, when upholding the lineage of our school, one must distinguish between gain and loss."

Furthermore, Daci recognized the illness [of the monks] and did not answer their questions; when a monk came forward, he would simply return to his quarters. Xuedou recognized the illness and did not answer their questions;
if a monk came forward, he would strike them across the back with his staff. The masters of various regions recognized the illness and did not answer their questions;
if a monk came forward, they certainly possessed some other superior quality, for there was not one who dared to move. "In the Great Tang, there were only three such Emperors."
The Master said: "Daci recognizes the illness and does not answer the question. At that time, a monk stepped forward, and he immediately returned to his quarters.
Like a spark of flint or a flash of lightning—this is dull. Xuedou recognizes the illness and does not answer the question; if a monk steps forward, he strikes him across the spine.

Like a cliff standing ten thousand fathoms high—this is perilous. Yuyang recognizes the illness and does not answer the question; if a monk steps forward, he immediately descends from his meditation seat.
[The Master] stood up. "Is there anyone here who can distinguish between gain and loss?
He cited the case of Zhaozhou arriving at Huangbo. When Huangbo saw him coming, he immediately shut the door to his quarters. Zhaozhou cried out, "Put out the fire! Put out the fire!"
Huangbo came out, seized him, and said, "Speak! Speak! Baizhang said, "Drawing the bow after the thief has fled. Xuedou said, "Truly a laughable matter;
one could laugh for thirty years. Suddenly, there was a monk who asked Xuedou, "What is there to laugh at?"
The Master said, "Laughing bandits! Drawing the bow after the thief has fled.
These are three old thieves. Now tell me, which one is the real thief? Let those with the eye of discernment distinguish them."
A monk asked Jingqing, “The student has not yet reached the source; I beg the Master for a skillful means. Jingqing said, “What source? The monk said, “That very source.
Jingqing said, “If it is that very source, how can it receive a skillful means? Xuedou said, “It is submerged in dead water; what use is there in that?

An attendant asked, “Just now, did you not strip him bare? Jingqing said, “No. *Note: "成褫伊" (chéngchǐ yī) is interpreted here as "to strip him bare" or "to expose him," a common pedagogical term in Chan literature.*
The attendant said, "He has not yet removed his robes. Jingqing said, "No. The attendant asked, "What is your honorable intention, Master?
Jingqing said, "A single drop of ink and water forms two dragons. Xuedou said, "He is still a bit short of it. Xuedou did not mean to diminish Jingqing’s majestic brilliance;
rather, he wished to have this monk meet him face-to-face. What is that source? That source will be revealed thirty years hence.
"I would give you thirty blows.
The Master said: "When the mountain was nearly nine fathoms high, he failed to add even one basket of earth.

At that time, that monk should have waited for Jingqing to say, "If this is its source, how could it accept expedient means? He should have simply prostrated himself and departed. Would that not have been so?
"Surpassing those before and excelling those after. Since Jingqing’s efforts were thus in vain, he repeatedly suffered defeat at the hands of the attendant.
Xuedou said, "Thirty years hence, I shall give you thirty blows"—this is truly like swinging a club to strike the moon.
A monk asked Xianglin, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? Lin said, "In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains.
Xuedou said, "In the eleventh month, the mountains burn; ten thousand kinds and a thousand variations. The crane perches on the pine, cold; the man treading through snow, freezing.
Bodhidharma did not understand—what a great difficulty, what a great difficulty!"
The Master said: "When the mountains are burned in the twelfth month, the tiger’s coat is naturally striped. At the Hanyuan Palace, do not seek Chang'an.
He then cited Master Benren’s address to the assembly: "Ordinarily, I do not wish to dally with people's sons and daughters before sound or after a phrase.
Why? Because sound is not sound, and form is not form. At that time, a monk asked: "How is it..."
"This sound is not sound. Ren said, "Can you call it 'form'? The monk asked, "What is form that is not form?
Ren said, "Can you call it 'sound'? The monk bowed. Ren said, "Tell me, did I speak for you, or did I answer your question?
If one can discern this, there will be a point of entry. Xuedou said, "Benren was truly extraordinary; however—"
He greedily gazes at the heavens. Since it is neither before sound nor after words, how does one enter?
The Master said, "Benren, you say that sound is not sound and form is not form; is this not merely playing with people's sons and daughters?
Even the single word 'enter' is unnecessary. Xuedou said, "Since it is neither before sound nor after words..."
Later, how would you enter? Why such a frantic urgency?
[The Master] cites Yunmen’s address to the assembly: "When the World-Honored One was born, he pointed with one hand toward heaven and with the other toward earth;
he took seven steps and looked around in the four directions, saying, 'Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored. Had anyone seen him at that moment—"
"Strike him dead! Give it to the dog to eat, so that all under heaven may enjoy peace. Xuedou said, "I would have overturned the meditation seat right then.
The Master said, "Yunmen and Xuedou wish to walk hand-in-hand with Śākyamuni, yet they still fail to emerge [from their own limitations]."
He could not depict it.
The National Teacher called to his attendant three times. Xuedou said, "To point is to miss the mark.
When the attendant responded three times, Xuedou said, "To arrive is to fail to point. "I thought I was failing you; who knew you were failing me? Xuedou said.
Xuedou could not let this pass. Yunmen said, "What is the National Teacher’s point of failing the attendant?
Even if you understand it, it is groundless. Xuedou said, "So, he did not understand after all. Yunmen said, "What is the attendant?"
"Regarding the place where I have failed the National Teacher: even if my bones were ground to powder and my body shattered to pieces, I would not yet have repaid him.
Xuedou said, "Pointless, pointless. The Master said, "Three times he called out 'I owe you,' and three times he responded 'I owe you.
*Sulu xili, xili sulu.* Yunmen’s grinding his bones to powder and Xuedou’s slicing his heart to pieces—none of these have yet repaid the National Teacher. (He made a gesture.)
"How would you respond? He then called to his attendant. The attendant responded with a "Yes. "Thirty years from now," he said, "you must not let me down.
He further raised this case: A monk asked Touzi, "What was the meaning of the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant? Touzi said, "To suppress..."
“What are you trying to force someone to do? Xuedou said. “A fellow who relies on a crutch,” the Master said. “There is no portion for him to bite into. A monk asked Xinghua.
Xinghua said, “One blind man leads a crowd of blind men. Xuedou said, “Truly blind. The Master said, “He has added one more. A monk asked Xuansha.
Xuansha said, “The attendant understands, however. Xuedou said, “Imprisoning the prisoner increases his wisdom. The Master said, “Recognizing the servant.”
The Monk asked Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "It is like a person writing characters in the dark; though the characters are not formed, the traces of the brushstrokes are already manifest.
Xuedou then shouted. The Master [Zhaozhou] said, "The colors rush toward a petty man. A monk asked Xuedou, and Xuedou struck him.
The Master said, "Alas, you fellow Meng! Xuedou further offered this verse: "The meeting of teacher and disciple is no trivial matter;
Without a thing to do, they walk together through the weeds. Whether it be 'carrying you' or 'carrying me,' let none inquire; Let them compete for the headship of the world as they please."
The Master said: "Idle talk. When someone asked about the National Teacher of Yewang, who called his attendant three times, [the Master] replied to him:
"What marrow do you seek within a withered bone?"
A monk asked Master Zhimen, “What is the Buddha? Zhimen said, “Trampling through straw sandals, walking barefoot.
The monk asked, “What is the matter beyond the Buddha? Zhimen said, “Carrying the sun and moon upon the tip of my staff.
Xuedou said, “A thousand soldiers are easy to find; a single general is hard to seek.”
The Master said: "The straw sandals are worn through; the staff carries the sun and moon. A single general is hard to find, yet a thousand chariots share the same track.

He cited the founding Master’s question to Nanquan: "The *maṇi* jewel people do not recognize; it is intimately held within the *tathāgatagarbha*. What is the *tathāgatagarbha*? Nanquan said: "That which comes and goes with you, Old Teacher Wang, is the *garbha*. Xuedou said: [The Master said: "The straw sandals are worn through; the staff carries the sun and moon. A single general is hard to find, yet a thousand chariots share the same track. He cited the founding Master’s question to Nanquan: "The *maṇi* jewel people do not recognize;
it is intimately held within the *tathāgatagarbha*. What is the *tathāgatagarbha*? Nanquan said: "That which comes and goes with you, Old Teacher Wang, is the *garbha*. Xuedou said:
"A man from the weeds. Master Zhaozhou said, "That which neither comes nor goes. Yuanquan said, "This too is a concealment. Xuedou said, "Adding frost to snow.
Zhaozhou asked, "What is the pearl? Xuedou said, "Dangerous! To perform acrobatics atop a hundred-foot pole is not the work of a true master.
If you can apply the eye here, guest and host will interchange, and you will be able to penetrate deeply into the tiger's den. Or...
"Not so. Even if the Master and Patriarch had attained enlightenment, they would still be men whose heads are dragons but whose tails are snakes.
The Master said, "Nanquan sets sail with the current; Xuedou steers against the wind.
The Master and Patriarch failed to reach the village in front and missed the inn behind. When someone asked Yuyang, "What is the Tathāgatagarbha? he immediately said to him:
The mountains cut off doubt; there is no path. The stream winds back; there is another village. What is the pearl? I say: look beneath your feet. A monk bowed to Xuefeng.
Xuefeng struck him five blows. The monk said, "What fault have I committed? Xuefeng struck him another five blows. Xuedou said:
"Xuedou has never entangled himself in complications with others. As for the first five blows: the sun shines upon heaven."
"Facing it. Five blows later. "Clouds rise and rain falls. If you can discern this, I shall gladly give you five blows.
The Master said: "The first five blows: the stone ox guards the ancient path. The latter five blows:
one horse gives birth to three tigers. Xuedou is able to distinguish and differentiate; he has both rewards and punishments. He too deserves five blows.

To cite Master Mazu: he ordered Zhizang to deliver a letter to Mount Jing. When the Master of the Mountain (Zhaozhou) received the letter and opened it, he saw a perfect circle with a single dot placed within it.
National Teacher Huichang, upon hearing this report, said, "Master Qin was still deluded by Master Ma. Xuedou said:
It is enough that Jingshan was deluded; but if he had presented this to the National Teacher, what other skillful means could he have employed to avoid being deluded?
An old master said, "At that moment, he should have sat [in meditation] and left it at that. Others have also said, "He simply should have drawn a line through it."
If it is as you say, you are simply shameless. How dare you claim that the teachers of the world all possess the vajra-eye and can perform vast supernatural transformations;
even so, can you escape [this critique]? Xuedou’s insight is something I wish for everyone to know together.
When Master Ma made that sketch at that time, he was already deluded himself.
The Master said: "One person dwells in Jiangxi, one dwells in Zhexi, and one dwells in Nanyang; they are as far apart as a wind-blown horse and an ox-cow, unable to reach one another.
Why, then, did he utter a single word that confuses and disturbs the people of the world? Xuedou broke into a cold sweat.
His merit is great; his fame is not attained in vain. King Yuezhou dares to ask Xuedou: At that time, what aspect of reality did Mazu’s "perfect circle" (*yuanxiang*) clarify?
[Xuedou] cites Jingqing asking a monk: "Zhaozhou said, 'Go and drink tea. How do you understand this? The monk then went out. Jingqing—
Yunmen said, "A person from Handan learns the gait of Tang. Xuedou said, "This monk is not a person from Handan;
why does he learn the gait of Tang? If you can discern this, I will give you some tea to drink."
The Master said, "This monk has gone out. Is he enlightened or not? Xuedou said, "He is no man of Handan;
why does he imitate the gait of Tang? One must realize that this monk came directly from Zhaozhou.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the matter that lies beyond the Dharma-body? Yunmen said, "It is not difficult for me to tell you what lies beyond;
how do you understand the Dharma-body? The monk said, "I beg the Master to examine it for me.
Yunmen said, "Setting aside the examination for a moment, how do you understand the Dharma-body? The monk said, "Just so, just so. Yunmen said, "This is just the long bench [of the monastic hall]."
"What you have learned upon the meditation seat—let me ask you this: does the Dharmakāya eat rice? The monk was speechless.
Xuedou said, "He has nearly completed a mountain nine fathoms high, yet fails to add a single basket of earth. Where does the fault lie?"
The Master said: "If that monk, at that time, had waited for him to ask, 'Does the Dharma-body eat rice?
and had simply replied, 'The entire great earth is the rice; where would you, O Monk, set your teeth? then Yunmen would surely have retreated three thousand miles."
Xuedou said: "When a mountain nine fathoms high is about to be completed, yet one basketful of earth is not added—this applies to Yunmen’s portion, and it applies to this monk’s portion."
To cite the story of Zhaozhou visiting Zhunyu: As soon as he stepped onto the Dharma Hall, Zhunyu said, "Watch the arrow! Zhaozhou also said, "Watch the arrow!
Zhunyu said, "It has passed. Zhaozhou said, "I hit it. Xuedou said, "Both were masters. Yet, in truth, both Zhunyu and Zhaozhou were not masters; their arrow-points did not meet.
Even if they had fired in unison and hit the mark together, it would still have been nothing more than shooting at a target.
Han-shan said:
"The spark struck from flint, the flash of lightning—whether you grasp it or fail to grasp it, you cannot avoid losing your body and forfeiting your life.
Xuedou merely blinked his eyes. Do you wish to recognize Zhu-yu and Zhaozhou? They have long been accustomed to wandering before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion.
[The Master] said: "It is past. Holding a golden whip in his hand, he celebrates the Great Peace.
[The text] cites Linji and Puhua going to a donor’s house for a meal. Linji asked, "A hair swallows the vast ocean; a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru.
Is this the wondrous function of spiritual powers, or is it simply the natural state of things? Puhua kicked over the rice table.
Linji said, "You are too crude. Huangbo said, "What kind of place is this, where you speak of coarse or subtle?
Linji then desisted. On the following day, they again attended a donor’s vegetarian feast together. Linji asked once more, "How does today’s offering compare to yesterday's?
Huangbo again kicked over the dining table. Linji said, "You are truly crude. Huangbo said, "In the Buddha-dharma, what is there to call 'crude'?"
Xuefeng said, "Fine. Jietu then stuck out his tongue. Xuedou said, "These two old thieves have not even finished their meal;
they deserve twenty blows of the staff. Though the blows are dealt, tell me: which one is the real thief?"
The Master said: "Puhua employed the affairs of the sword’s edge; Linji could only stick out his tongue.
As for Xuedou’s twenty blows—was it a reward or a punishment?
He raised his *sanzhuo* staff to show the assembly, saying: "If one discusses this matter, the mere lifting of the eyebrows is already a missed opportunity. Magu...
Xuedou said: "He missed it—let us not speak of that. What is this matter? Jue said: "He missed it.
Gu then overturned the meditation seat, and Jue struck him. Xuedou said: "These two headless, tailless fellows;
their eyebrows have not even blinked. Why speak of 'missing' this matter? A monk asked: 'Why do the eyebrows not blink?'"
Xuedou struck him immediately.
The Master said: "A single drop of water from a triangle can swell into waves that reach the heavens.
Magu tried to scoop it all up in one gulp, unaware that his nostrils were being soaked and rotted away. Xuedou, not sparing a single eyebrow, sought to clarify this."
In this matter, it is as if something is pressing and constricting beneath one’s heels.
When Muzhou called out to a monk, “Virtuous One,” the monk turned his head; Muzhou said, “A fellow carrying a wooden board.
Xuedou said, “Muzhou possesses only one eye. Why? When that monk turned his head at being called, why did he end up becoming a ‘board-carrying’ fellow?”
The Master said: "This single board—Muzhou carries one side, Xuedou carries the other side; it has nothing at all to do with this monk's business.

Just as he had finished his prostrations, [Dongshan] struck him across the back. This not only cut through Dongshan’s doubts but also firmly grasped the old master Huineng.
Do you understand? General Li has a glorious reputation; that he did not receive a fief as a marquis was merely a matter of circumstance.
The Master said: "Jade is naturally without flaw; to carve patterns upon it is to lose its virtue.
He then cited Ba Ling’s address to the assembly: "The Patriarch said, 'It is not the wind moving, nor is it the banner moving.
Since it is neither the banner nor the wind, where does it reside? If there is anyone who can act as the Patriarch's advocate, come forth and engage with Ba Ling."
[Zhaozhou] said, “I see. Xuedou said, “Xuedou says: ‘The wind moves, the banner moves. Since they are both wind and banner, where can you place them?
If there is someone who acts as a patron for Baling, let them also come forth and meet with Xuedou.
The Master said, "A pair of unperforated iron hammers.
Once, while Mazu and Layman Pang were picking tea, the Layman said, "The Dharma-realm admits no person; do you still see me, Master?
Mazu replied, "If it were not for you, Master, I would have already answered Layman Pang. The Layman said, "There is questioning and there is answering..."
The Master replied, "This is merely routine; I do not concern myself with it. The scholar said, "Was it not because you did not take offense when I just now questioned you?
The Master again ignored him. The scholar shouted, "You ill-mannered fellow! Wait until I present this one by one to someone with clear eyes!
The Master picked up his tea basket and went straight back. Xuedou said, "Thus, Master Chuanshan only knew how to hold fast to his own borders; he could not..."
"Born together and dying together. At that time, he should have simply pulled off his head-wrap (*fùtóu*). Who would dare call him Layman Pang? The Master said:
"Layman Pang took the path and went; he was too hasty in his journey. Once a word has left the mouth, even four horses cannot overtake it.
At that moment, he should have waited for him to say, "Wait until I have presented each and every point to those with clear eyes."
It requires nothing more than to say: "Tomorrow there shall be no general labor. This not only cuts off Pang’s path, but also spares Xuedou from stirring up a wind on his grass mat.
[The Master] cites a monk asking Yunmen: "When a single word expresses it all, what then? Yunmen said: "Torn asunder. Xuedou snapped his fingers.
[The Master] struck three times.
He said, "How well you sing the *zhègū* [partridge] song in the spring breeze!
He cited a monk who asked Muzhou, "What is it like when a single word expresses everything? Muzhou replied, "The old monk is in your alms-bag."
[The Master] said, "Inside. Xuedou laughed loudly.
The Master said, "The ox's head points south; the horse's head points north.
He then raised up Master Bensheng’s staff and said to the assembly, "If I were to lift it up, you would immediately turn toward what has not yet been lifted."
"When it arises, act with principle. If I do not pick it up, you will then attempt to exercise mastery over the very moment of its arising.
Tell me, where does this old monk stand in relation to people? At that time, a monk came forward and said, "I dare not arbitrarily create complications.
Yunmen said, "I know the Acharya does not go beyond the ordinary. The monk said, "At the lowest point, there is still room for leveling; at the highest point," [he left the sentence unfinished].
"Observing this is not enough," Sheng said. "A joint upon a joint has grown. The monk remained silent.

Sheng said, "Covering one's nose while stealing fragrance; one reaps only the guilt. Xuedou said, "This monk was indeed skilled at critical inquiry, yet alas, his bow is broken and his arrows exhausted.
Nevertheless, Master Bensheng was a true master; when he raised [his hand], heaven turned and earth revolved."
Turn! You must fold your hands in submission and lay down your burden; do not continue to walk against the wind.
You must surely withdraw your whole being to avoid harm, yet will you still see the place where your original birth as a human being resides? Again, he took up his staff and said:
"Peace is originally brought about by the generals, yet it is not permitted for the generals to witness that peace."

The Master said: "In the original birth, there is seizing and releasing; there is letting go and gathering in. This monk intended to pass through the Dragon Gate, yet he was struck on the forehead once more.
What is it like at the point where the bow is broken and the arrows exhausted? The moon is like a drawn bow; little rain, much wind."
A monk asked Xuefeng, "It is said that when a Śrāvaka perceives their nature, it is like seeing the moon at night; when a Bodhisattva perceives their nature, it is like seeing the sun by day.
I wonder, Master, how do you perceive your nature? Xuefeng struck him three times. The monk then asked Yantou the same question, and Yantou slapped him three times.
Xuedou said, "He prescribed medicine according to the illness and gave him three blows. But if we were to follow the rule..."
As they were walking together, [Xuefeng] asked, "How many times should we strike?
The Master said: "Seeing the moon at night is the perspective of the Śrāvaka; seeing the sun by day is the perspective of the Bodhisattva.
Xuefeng’s three blows are Xuefeng’s perspective; Yantou’s three slaps are Yantou’s perspective."
Why do you monks not understand this? Xuedou acts according to the mandate; he too is a fellow who plays with lumps of mud.
Take the case of Upāsaka Fu of Taiyuan, who went to visit Xuefeng. Upon reaching the Dharma Hall, he looked at Xuefeng and then immediately went down to attend to the administrative affairs.
Xuedou said: "A master of the school among fifteen hundred men—yet upon being glanced at by Old Fu, he was [defeated]."
He hoisted his flag high and lowered it again. On the following day, he entered the abbot’s quarters and said, "Yesterday I offended the Master.
Yunfeng said, "Knowing it was such a matter, leave it at that. Xuedou said, "As expected. A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the point of having offended him? Yunmen struck him.
Xuedou said, "Even if you strike a hundred thousand or ten million people like this, what use is there? It is simply—"
"Only when all the people on the great earth have been struck with the staff can Xuefeng be truly established. But tell me, what kind of eye does Taoyuan Fu possess?
The Master said, "Taoyuan Fu is like a dragon gaining the water; old Xuefeng is like a tiger relying on the mountain. Yunmen cut him off.
Iron cuts through nails. Xuedou drags along mud and water. I, this mountain monk, wish to ask Xuedou:
what is the place where Xuefeng hoisted high his banner of surrender? Where the level marshes end, there are green mountains; the traveler lies even further beyond the green mountains.
An-guo raised the question and asked the monk, "If one attains it within the mind, even *eranda* (Ilan) becomes a sandalwood tree;
if one loses the essential meaning, even nectar becomes a garden of thorns. I want a phrase that encompasses both the attainment and the loss.
The monk held up his fist and said, "It cannot be called a 'fist'. An-guo said, "Precisely because it is called a 'fist' [it is so]. Xuedou commented, "No rope."
"A man who binds himself does not even recognize his own fist.
The Master said, "An-guo is like one who fixes the leather pegs while tuning the strings; Xue-dou is like one who knocks at empty space to seek a sound.
Even if one were to achieve both gain and loss perfectly, it would still be nothing more than the cleverness of a child."
The Verse-Commentary on the Ancient Case cites Emperor Wu of Liang, who asked Master Bodhidharma, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?
Bodhidharma replied, "Vast and empty; there is no sage. The Emperor said, "Who is it that stands before me? Bodhidharma replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not attain realization.
He then crossed the river and went to Wei. The verse says: "Vast and empty, there is no sage;
Prescribing medicine according to the ailment. To say 'I do not know' once more, Is to strip it all away with total sincerity.
Raising the white jade mallet, Yet it is but a golden chisel. Coming ten thousand miles from the West— This is the blow that strikes the head. Yet he leaves behind but a single shoe."
He did not take it back; to this day it remains hanging from the corner of the Dragon Bed.
Quoting Zhaozhou’s address to the assembly, he said: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it simply dislikes picking and choosing.
As soon as there is speech, there is picking and choosing, and there is clarity. I, the old monk, do not dwell within clarity. Do you, then, cherish and protect it or not?"
At that time, a monk asked, "If you are not within clarity, what is there to guard and cherish?
Dazhou said, "I do not know either. The monk said, "Since the Master does not know, why do you say he is not within clarity?"
Zhaozhou said: "If you ask about a matter, you may do so; once you have finished your prostrations, withdraw.

He then offered this verse: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; It is like an iron wall and a silver mountain. If one has not yet clarified the meaning of the Three Patriarchs, It is hard to pass through Zhaozhou’s Barrier.
Within the clarity of discernment, Who would know it is as black as lacquer? Yet he says, 'I do not know'— Such repeated words are not worth consuming."

When Mazu Daishi was unwell, the head of the monastery asked him, "How has your health been lately, Master? Mazu replied, "The Buddha of the Sun’s Face, the Buddha of the Moon’s Face. The verse says: The Buddha of the Sun’s Face, the Buddha of the Moon’s Face— In the midst of illness, he reveals his true countenance. Though the body may be weary and the spirit faint, The Way is not something that can be grasped. If you wish to see the Great Master, Look at the sun and the moon. The verse says: The Buddha of the Sun’s Face, the Buddha of the Moon’s Face— In the midst of illness, he reveals his true countenance. Though the body may be weary and the spirit faint, The Way is not something that can be grasped. If you wish to see the Great Master, Look at the sun and the moon.
Sūryamukha Buddha, Candramukha Buddha; the person of no rank, bare bones and skin. The Great Statue of Jiazhou eats too much salt;
the Iron Ox of Shanzhou only increases its thirst. *Alala!* The hundred rivers flow backward in a tumultuous din.
The Record of Deqing Shan’s visit to Weishan: Carrying his outer robe and bowl, he walked from the west side to the east side of the Dharma Hall, and from the east side to the west side.
Looking around, he said, “Nothing, nothing,” and then departed. When he reached the entrance of the gate, he turned back and said, “One must not act so hastily.
He then assumed his formal demeanor and entered again for an audience. While Weishan was seated, Deqing Shan brought forth [his staff].
As he was rising from his seat, he said, "Preceptor. As Guishan reached for his whisk, Deshan let out a shout, shook out his sleeves, and departed.
With his back turned to the Dharma Hall, Deshan put on his straw sandals and left. That evening, Guishan asked the Head Seat:
"Where was that newcomer who just arrived? The Head Seat replied, "At that moment, he turned his back on the Dharma Hall and went out wearing straw sandals.

Guishan said, "In the future, this fellow will go off to the summit of a solitary peak, build a grass hut, and there he will revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs. He then offered this verse: He turns his back on the Dharma Hall, And goes out wearing straw sandals.
In the future, upon a solitary peak, He will build a grass hut and revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs.
Deqiao seeks a wrestling match before the horse; Guishan draws his bow after the thief has fled.
Meeting atop a solitary peak, they are two great, hairless tigers.

Xuefeng raised his staff and addressed the assembly, saying: "The entire great earth is gathered up and made as small as a grain of millet; it is tossed before you, yet you, you lacquer buckets, do not understand. Let us strike the drum and invite everyone to look! He then spoke this verse: The entire great earth is gathered up, Reduced to the size of a grain of millet;
Tossed before you, you lacquer buckets— You do not understand! Strike the drum and let us all look together.
To gather up the great earth as if it were a grain of millet—the old man Xuefeng has needlessly exhausted his spirit.
How much better to roll out three balls and catch the man upon the fishing boat!
Citing Master Yunmen, he uttered these words: "I will not ask you about the period before the fifteenth day;
tell me a phrase for the period after the fifteenth day. [Yunmen] spoke on his behalf: "Every day is a good day. The verse says:
Every day is a fine day. One’s entire being resides in the imperial capital. Along the flower-lined avenues and willow-strewn paths, travelers are busy celebrating the spring outing.
Cattle are let loose in the wilds of Peach Grove; horses return to the southern slopes of Mount Hua. One knows not where the boundaries of territory lie.
A monk asked Fayan: "Huishao asks the Master, 'What is the Buddha? Fayan said, "You are Huishao. The verse says:
Qingxi directly points to the source; Tides strike the empty city, waves lap the sky. Great and small Huishao alike remain asleep.
He replied, "I am the Immortal of Wine.
He then cited the occasion when Cuiyan addressed the assembly at the end of the summer retreat, saying: "Throughout this entire summer, I have been speaking with you, my brothers.
Look—do Cuiyan’s eyebrows still remain? Baofu said, "The heart of a thief is always fearful. Changqing said, "They grow! Yunmen said, "They are gone."
Yunmen said, "A barrier. The verse says:
Cuiyan, Changqing, Yunmen, and Baofu— Those aboard the same boat act as enemies to one another.
Eyebrows fall away entirely only to grow back again; Both nostrils and eyes are utterly lost.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is Zhaozhou? Zhaozhou replied, “The east gate, the south gate, the west gate, the north gate. Verse:
East gate, south gate, West gate, north gate. When the east wind stirs, the horse’s hooves race; In a single day, one surveys the entire length.
An-chun. He raised the case of Muzhou asking a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk then shouted. Muzhou said, "I, this old monk, have been given a shout by you.
The monk shouted again. Muzhou said, "After three shouts and four shouts, what then? The monk was speechless. Muzhou—
He then struck him, saying, "This fellow who plunders empty space! The verse says:
"The blade of the vajra-jewel sword is blunt; Even the crouching lion must remain still.
It was not that the General boasted of his skillful hand, But he nearly shattered the city of Muzhou."
Master Huangbo addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you here are nothing but fellows who eat the dregs of wine.
Traveling as monks like this, how can you expect to have a future? Do you realize that within the Great Tang Empire there are no Chan masters?
At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked, "As for those in other quarters who guide their disciples and lead assemblies, what of them? Huangbo replied, "None."
The Way has no Chan; it is simply that there is no teacher. The verse says:
In the Great Tang Empire, there are no Chan masters; those who merely consume dregs of wine number as many as the sands of the Ganges. Before the Twelve Peaks lies an ancient adept;
thorny brambles reach the heavens, leaving no path to tread. (A shout!)
A monk asked Dongshan, “What is the Buddha? Dongshan replied, “Three pounds of flax. The verse says:
The first phrase is beyond deliberation; Those with true skill have always surpassed their peers.
Bringing forth Yunmen’s “dry turd,” Half a pound and eight ounces—exactly equal.
A monk asked Baling, "What is the school of Deva? Baling replied, "Snow in a silver bowl. The verse says: Snow in a silver bowl;
the Master’s vision was unerring. In the Western Heavens there are many of this kind; in the Eastern Land they are as numerous as hemp seeds.

Speaking thus to one, there is no error or confusion. When Hanshan meets Shide, they clap their hands and laugh "he-he.

A monk asked Yunmen: "It is not the mechanism before one's eyes, nor is it the matter before one's eyes. What is it like at such a time? Yunmen said: "Turn it upside down. The verse says: It is not the mechanism before one's eyes, Nor is it the matter before one's eyes.
If you wish to know the meaning of this, Just turn it upside down.
To speak of it in reverse is far too clear; the enlightened must know that there is a shock in the darkness. Before black and white have been distinguished, who can vie for the first move?
The wind and moon over the Five Lakes—whom do they belong to?

A monk asked Jingqing, "The student 'sips' [the air]; I pray the Master 'pecks' [it]. Jingqing said, "Will it still live? The monk said, "If it does not live, one will be ridiculed by others. Jingqing said, "He is also just a fellow from among the weeds. The verse says: The student sips; the Master pecks. If it does not live, it will be laughed at. Even so, he is but a fellow from among the weeds. How can the two birds ever meet? The golden-haired lion roars; The jade rabbit leaps. In the vast expanse of the blue sky, Who is there to witness it? The spring breeze blows over the ten directions; The autumn moon shines through the three realms. The ancient mirror reflects all things clearly; The bright pearl rolls freely. When the dragon’s roar shakes the heavens, The phoenix soars high. The great function is manifest; The subtle meaning is revealed. If you can understand this, You will see that the Way is not far off. If you cannot yet comprehend it, You must look within your own mind. Do not seek it outside yourself; It is right here before your eyes. The ancient Buddhas have already transmitted it; The patriarchs have already pointed it out. If you can grasp it in an instant, You will transcend the world of birth and death. If you hesitate for even a moment, You will fall into the pit of delusion. This is the true teaching of the Buddhas and patriarchs; This is the ultimate path of the sages. Do not doubt it; Do not hesitate. Straightforwardly, without artifice, Enter the gate of liberation. Thus, the verse concludes: The student sips; the Master pecks. If you can see this clearly, Then the whole world is the Great Way. If you do not see this clearly, You will wander lost in the three realms. Do not seek it outside yourself; Look within your own mind. If you can understand this, Then you have attained the ancestral mind. If you cannot understand this, You will remain a common person. If you do not see this clearly, You will remain trapped in samsara. Do not seek it in external forms; It is right here within your own nature. If you can understand this, Then you have realized the Buddha-mind. If you do not understand this, You will remain a wandering ghost. Regarding Liu Tiemo: When he arrived at Guishan, Guishan said, "Old cow, you have come. Tiemo replied, "Tomorrow there is a great assembly for a vegetarian feast at Mount Tai; will you, Preceptor, go as well? Guishan lay down, stretching out his body.

Tiemo then departed. The verse says: The old cow arrives at the mountain gate; Guishan calls her by name. She asks about the feast at Mount Tai; The Master lies down in silence. The sound of the hoofprints vanishes; The path of the tracks is lost. The great assembly is held within the house; Who can fathom its depth?
Though this cow is old, she has not yet grown decrepit; she goes to Mount Tai in the morning and returns by evening. I am weary and wish to sleep;
you may depart for now. If you have the intention tomorrow, come to the vegetarian feast.
The Master of Lotus Flower Peak raised his staff and addressed the assembly, saying: "When the ancients reached this point, why did they refuse to stay?
The assembly was silent. He said himself, "It is because on their paths they could not gain strength. He spoke again: "Ultimately, how is it? Then he said himself:
"Carrying my staff slung across my shoulder, heedless of others, I enter into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks."
He departs. The verse says:
The great capacity breaks forth, shaking the fundamental principles; Shouldering the staff, he enters the chaotic peaks. The rocks split and the cliffs collapse;
the path is cut off. A ten-fathom lotus flower shines crimson against the heavens.

The monk said, "If so, then it follows along with it. Sui said, "I follow it. The verse says: The kalpa-fire blazes, the world is consumed; The monk asks, "Is this destroyed? Sui replies, "It is destroyed.

The monk says, "Then it follows along. Sui says, "I follow it. In the midst of the fire, there is no place to hide; Only by following along can one transcend. If you do not follow along, you are lost; To follow along is to be free from all bonds. The ancient sages have already gone; Who is there to be followed? If you wish to see the Buddha, Look at the face of the monk.
The great trichiliocosm is a single void, blazing with fire; suddenly emerges an old, toothless tiger.
Raising the three-cornered eye of the monk, there is nowhere left to seek its tracks.

Once, Changsha returned from a day-long excursion in the mountains. Upon reaching the gate, the Head Seat asked, "Where have you been, Master?

Changsha said, "I have come back from wandering in the mountains. The Head Seat asked, "To what places did you go? Changsha said, "At first I followed the fragrant grasses away; then I returned, chasing the falling petals.
The Head Seat remarked, "That is very much like the spirit of spring. Changsha said, "It is also superior to the autumn dew."
Drops fall upon the lotus. The verse says:
Meeting on a narrow path, the family style is fully displayed; first following the fragrant grasses away, then returning with the falling petals.

The Head Seat adds luster; Changsha’s aspiration remains undimmed. A lotus droplets autumn dew; let not the patch-robed monks harbor suspicion. if it moves, it is sealed; if it stays, it is broken. What about when it neither moves nor stays—is that it?"

I request that the Master not apply the seal. Fengxue said, "Accustomed to fishing for whales and leviathans in vast depths, yet you sigh over the frog's stride in the mud and sand.

To illustrate this, consider the conversation between Grand Master Lu Xun and Nanquan. While they were conversing, the Grand Master remarked, "Master Zhao said that heaven and earth share the same root and all things are one body;
how truly marvelous! Nanquan pointed to a flower in the courtyard and called out to the Grand Master.
It is said: "People of that time saw this single stalk of flowers as if it were a dream.
The verse says: Heaven and earth share the same root; the myriad things are one body. A mangy horse is tied to a withered post; a black ox lies in dead water.
Old Teacher Wuzhuo has too much of a beak; he plucks the flower from their eyes. Boundless wind and flow emerge from the house of the lineage.

Citing Zhaozhou’s question to Touzi: "When one who has died the great death comes back to life, what is it like? Touzi said: "Night travel is not permitted; you must arrive at dawn. The verse says: Night travel is not permitted; At dawn, one must arrive.
The body is cold and stiff, The mind is clear and bright. The old man of Zhaozhou Is truly a rare sight. If you wish to see him, Look at the mountain peak.

To die greatly and then return to life—this is the refinement of consciousness. When the light breaks, you must arrive; do not permit yourself to travel by night. This is not because it is difficult to dwell with others;
rather, it is because, for the most part, the distinction between the monastic and the lay must be clear.

A monk asked Master Dongshan, “When cold and heat arrive, how can one avoid them? Dongshan said, “Why not go to a place where there is neither cold nor heat?

The monk asked, “What is the place where there is neither cold nor heat? Dongshan said, “When it is cold, let the cold kill you; when it is hot, let the heat kill you. The verse says: When cold and heat arrive, Where can one find refuge? If you seek a place beyond them, You will never find it.
